alphonsus-liguori.heroSummary: St. Alphonsus Liguori (1696–1787) was a Neapolitan lawyer who became a priest, founded the Redemptorists in 1732 to preach to the rural poor, and served as bishop of Sant'Agata dei Goti. Pius XII named him patron of confessors and moral theologians. A Doctor of the Church, he is celebrated on August 1.
alphonsus-liguori.searchDescription: St. Alphonsus Liguori (1696–1787), feast August 1: lawyer turned priest, Redemptorist founder, Doctor of the Church and patron of confessors.

symbols.meaning: His devotion to Christ in the Eucharist and his popular book of Visits to the Blessed Sacrament; Catholic Culture notes he is shown praying with a monstrance in his hands.
His many writings, from moral theology for confessors to devotional books written for ordinary people, which led to his being named a Doctor of the Church in 1871.
His preaching of Christ's love shown on the cross, the heart of the parish missions he and the Redemptorists gave.
His devotion to Mary, which he spread through works such as The Glories of Mary.

symbols.symbol: Bishop bent forward, chin on his chest
symbols.meaning: The painful illness of his later years, which led him to resign his diocese; Catholic Culture lists him among patrons against arthritis.

alphonsus-liguori.whyWeTurn: People turn to Alphonsus when they need mercy explained in plain words. He left a promising legal career, spent his life preaching to farmers and shepherds whom others overlooked, and wrote short, warm books so that anyone could learn to pray. As a moral theologian he resisted the harsh rigorism of his day and urged confessors to be faithful to Church teaching yet gentle with penitents, as Benedict XVI noted. Catholic Culture lists him as a patron against scrupulosity, and anxious consciences still find relief in him. Priests ask his help in the confessional, and ordinary Catholics in prayer.

quotes.text: He who prays is certainly saved. He who prays not is certainly damned.
quotes.work: The Great Means of Salvation and of Perfection, Part I, chapter 1, conclusion
quotes.translation: Centenary Edition, ed. Eugene Grimm, C.Ss.R. (1886), public domain

quotes.text: Because with the Lord there is mercy: and with him plentiful redemption.
quotes.work: Psalm 129:7 (130:7), source of the Redemptorist motto he chose, Copiosa apud eum redemptio

prayer.text: My Jesus, I believe that thou art present in the most holy sacrament. I love thee above all things: I desire to receive thee into my soul. Since I cannot now receive thee sacramentally, come at least spiritually into my heart. I embrace thee, and I unite myself entirely to thee, as if thou hadst already come: do not permit me to be ever separated from thee.
prayer.source: St. Alphonsus Liguori, Visits to the Most Holy Sacrament, introduction, "An Act for Spiritual Communion" (English translation by "a Catholic clergyman," New York: Catholic Publication Society, c. 1870), checked against the scanned text at the Internet Archive
prayer.note: This is the act of spiritual communion found in Alphonsus's own Visits to the Blessed Sacrament. Many modern prayer cards use slightly different wording (for example adding "truly" or "never permit me"); the text here follows the nineteenth-century translation exactly.

link.label: Read Visits to the Most Holy Sacrament (scanned edition, Internet Archive)

feastCustoms: Attend Mass on August 1, his memorial in the General Roman Calendar.
Make a visit to the Blessed Sacrament and pray his act of spiritual communion, the practice his Visits book was written to encourage.
Go to confession, and pray for priests who hear confessions, since Pius XII named him patron of confessors.
Read his short work Uniformity with God's Will, which Catholic Culture recommends for his feast.
Listen to or sing Tu scendi dalle stelle, the Italian Christmas carol Benedict XVI credits to him.

alphonsus-liguori.confirmationNote: Alphonsus suits a Confirmation candidate who is practical, organized, or drawn to law, writing, or helping people who are overlooked. He gave up a successful career to serve the poor, and he spent his life making the faith simple and merciful without making it less true. Choosing his name can be a commitment to regular prayer, frequent confession, and patience with others.
reflectionPrompts: Do I picture God as harsh or as merciful, and what has shaped that picture?
This week, stop by a church for five minutes before the Blessed Sacrament, or pray an act of spiritual communion each day.
Read Benedict XVI's general audience on St. Alphonsus (March 30, 2011), then the conclusion of chapter 1 of The Great Means of Salvation in the Centenary Edition.

ambrose.heroSummary: St. Ambrose of Milan (about 340–397) was a Roman governor who was acclaimed bishop of Milan in 374 while still a catechumen. He preached, wrote hymns, ransomed captives with church gold, and baptized St. Augustine. A Doctor of the Church, he is celebrated on December 7, the day he was ordained bishop.
ambrose.searchDescription: St. Ambrose of Milan, feast December 7: Roman governor acclaimed bishop in 374, hymn writer, Doctor of the Church, and the bishop who baptized Augustine.

symbols.meaning: His sweet, persuasive preaching, which earned him the title "Honey-Tongued Doctor"; a legend says a swarm of bees settled on his mouth when he was a baby, an omen of his eloquence.
His firmness in defending the faith against Arianism and in calling even an emperor to penance; Catholic Culture notes the whip often has three thongs for the Trinity.
His more than twenty years as bishop of Milan, which began with his ordination on December 7.
His writings on Scripture, the sacraments, and Christian duty, which place him among the four great Latin Doctors of the Church.
The relics of the martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, which Augustine records Ambrose found in Milan in 386.

ambrose.whyWeTurn: People turn to Ambrose when they are handed a responsibility they did not seek. He was a civil governor, not yet baptized, when the people of Milan demanded him as bishop, and he answered by studying Scripture, giving his wealth to the poor, and preaching often. He melted church vessels to free captives and told an emperor to do public penance. Augustine wrote that Ambrose received him like a father, and his sermons helped bring Augustine to faith. Students, teachers, preachers, and anyone thrust into leadership can ask his help to serve with courage and a generous heart.

quotes.text: The Church has gold, not to store up, but to lay out, and to spend on those who need.
quotes.work: On the Duties of the Clergy (De Officiis), Book II, chapter 28, §137
quotes.translation: H. de Romestin, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 10 (1896), public domain

quotes.text: Maker of all, the Lord, / And Ruler of the height, / Who, robing day in light, hast poured / Soft slumbers o'er the night
quotes.work: His evening hymn Deus Creator omnium, as quoted by Augustine in Confessions, Book IX, chapter 12

quotes.text: To him was I unknowing led by Thee, that by him I might knowingly be led to Thee. That man of God received me as a father, and showed me an Episcopal kindness on my coming.
quotes.work: St. Augustine, Confessions, Book V, chapter 13, on meeting Ambrose in Milan

prayer.text: Lord God, you called St. Ambrose from public office to shepherd your people, and he answered with study, prayer, and generosity. When I am given work I did not expect, help me to learn what I need and to serve faithfully. Make me free with what I own, so that people in need come before my possessions. Give me courage to speak the truth with charity, even to the powerful. Through his prayers, bless all bishops, teachers, and students, and draw restless hearts to you as you drew Augustine through his preaching. Amen.

In Milan, December 7 is the feast of the city's patron, and the Archdiocese of Milan still celebrates the Ambrosian Rite that bears his name.
Give something to people in need, or support work for prisoners and captives, remembering his teaching that the Church's gold is for those who need it.
Pray his evening hymn "Maker of all" before sleep, as Augustine did after his mother's death.
Bake honey cakes or share honey in honor of the "Honey-Tongued Doctor," a Catholic Culture suggestion for the day.

ambrose.confirmationNote: Ambrose suits a Confirmation candidate who has been asked to lead, or who loves public speaking, law, or history. He did not feel ready to be a bishop, yet he learned the Scriptures, gave away his wealth, and stood up for the faith and the poor. Choosing his name can be a commitment to keep learning, to serve generously, and to speak the truth with courage.
reflectionPrompts: Where am I being asked to take responsibility before I feel ready, and what would it mean to trust God with it?
Choose one possession or sum of money you could share this week, and give it to someone in real need.
Read Augustine's Confessions, Book V, chapter 13 and Book VI, chapter 3, then Benedict XVI's general audience on St. Ambrose (October 24, 2007).

anastasia.heroSummary: St. Anastasia of Sirmium is an early Christian martyr remembered for helping Christians persecuted under Diocletian. Her name stands in the Roman Canon among seven women martyrs, and her commemoration on December 25 links her to the Christmas Mass at Dawn. Little about her life is documented; her detailed passion story comes from later tradition.
anastasia.searchDescription: St. Anastasia of Sirmium, martyr under Diocletian, is named in the Roman Canon and remembered on December 25 with the Christmas Mass at Dawn.

symbols.meaning: The traditional sign of a martyr's victory, marking her death for Christ.

symbols.symbol: Flame, held in her hand or in a bowl
symbols.meaning: Her death by burning, as her passion story relates it.
The faith in Christ she refused to renounce after her arrest.
Usually connected with the care she gave to persecuted Christians; the exact origin of this attribute comes from tradition and is not explained in the Catholic sources consulted.

anastasia.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Anastasia when faith begins to cost something. Her memory starts with practical help: she cared for Christians suffering in the persecution of Diocletian and then shared their fate. Tradition holds that she was arrested at Sirmium, escaped from a sinking ship, was taken again and was burned alive. Little else is certain, yet by the fifth century Rome honored her, and her name is still spoken in the Roman Canon. Many Catholics meet her at Christmas, when her quiet memory sits beside the joy of the Nativity. She reminds us to remember prisoners and all who suffer for Christ, and to stay faithful ourselves.

quotes.text: Naked, and you covered me: sick, and you visited me: I was in prison, and you came to me.
Remember them that are in bands, as if you were bound with them; and them that labour, as being yourselves also in the body.

prayer.text: St. Anastasia, you cared for Christians who were imprisoned and afraid, and you did not abandon Christ when your own turn came. Pray for all who suffer for their faith today, and for everyone behind bars who feels forgotten. At Christmas, when we celebrate the Light that came into the world, help me to notice those who sit in darkness. Give me the courage to visit, to write, to give and to speak for them. Keep me faithful when following Jesus costs me something, and let my care for others be a gift laid before the Child of Bethlehem. Amen.

feastCustoms: On Christmas Day, attend the Mass at Dawn. In the older form of the Roman Rite it includes a commemoration of St. Anastasia, and Rome's traditional station for that Mass is her church, Sant'Anastasia al Palatino.
When the priest uses Eucharistic Prayer I (the Roman Canon), listen for her name among the women martyrs remembered after the consecration.
Eastern Catholics and others who follow the Byzantine calendar keep her memory on December 22, so you can begin remembering her before Christmas.
Remember prisoners during the Christmas season: send a card or gift through a parish or diocesan prison ministry, or support one financially.
Pray for Christians who are persecuted for their faith today.
anastasia.confirmationNote: Anastasia can suit a confirmand drawn to quiet, practical courage. Her name comes from the Greek word for resurrection, fitting for a sacrament that completes the new life begun in Baptism. The Church remembers her for helping persecuted Christians and for staying faithful after her own arrest, and her name is still heard in the Roman Canon. Choosing her is a commitment to stand beside people who suffer for their faith.
reflectionPrompts: Who in your life is 'in bands' right now, whether imprisoned, ill or trapped by circumstances, and how could you remember them this week?
Before Christmas, write to someone in prison through a parish or diocesan prison ministry, or give to one.
Read Matthew 25:31–46 and Hebrews 13:1–3, and note what each passage asks of Christians toward those in prison.

andr-bessette.heroSummary: St. André Bessette was a Holy Cross brother in Montreal who spent almost forty years as a college doorkeeper and sent the troubled and sick who came to him to St. Joseph. From that ministry grew Saint Joseph's Oratory on Mount Royal. Canonized in 2010, he is celebrated on January 7 in Canada and January 6 in the United States.
andr-bessette.searchDescription: St. André Bessette, Holy Cross brother and doorkeeper, led the sick to St. Joseph and inspired Saint Joseph's Oratory in Montreal. Feast: January 6 or 7.

symbols.meaning: His assignment in 1871 as doorkeeper at Collège Notre-Dame, where he served for almost forty years and welcomed everyone who came.

symbols.symbol: Lamp and oil of St. Joseph
symbols.meaning: He took oil from a lamp burning before St. Joseph and invited the sick to use it while praying; the Oratory keeps that practice alive.
The saint he pointed every visitor toward; he kept a small statue of Joseph on his windowsill and insisted that Joseph, not he, did the healing.
His heart is preserved as a relic at the Oratory, presented there as a sign of his love for God and compassion for others.

andr-bessette.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. André when they are sick, worn out or carrying more than they can manage. He was an orphan who tried many trades without much success before his community gave him one of its humblest jobs: answering the door. He made that door a place of welcome, listening to people in trouble, praying with them and sending them to St. Joseph. Healings were attributed to that prayer, but André kept repeating that St. Joseph was the one who cured. Asking his help is a way of bringing ordinary burdens to God with simple trust, and of learning that no task is too small to serve Christ in others.

quotes.text: Go to Joseph: and do all that he shall say to you.
quotes.work: Genesis 41:55 (Pharaoh's words about the patriarch Joseph, echoed in the devotion 'Ite ad Joseph' that André made his own)

quotes.text: Naked, and you covered me: sick, and you visited me: I was in prison, and you came to me.

prayer.text: St. André, faithful doorkeeper, you welcomed everyone who knocked and listened to their troubles with patience. Teach me to open the door of my heart to those who come to me tired, sick or afraid. Lead me, as you led so many, to St. Joseph, who guarded Jesus and Mary and cares for all who call on him. Pray for the sick, for those who care for them, and for everyone who feels that their work is small and unseen. Help me to trust that God can do great things through humble service. Amen.

feastCustoms: Keep his feast: January 7 in Canada and at Saint Joseph's Oratory, and January 6 as an optional memorial in the United States.
Visit, call or run an errand for someone who is sick or homebound, and offer to pray with them, as André did.
Ask St. Joseph's intercession for a particular need. The Oratory still keeps oil burning before a statue of St. Joseph and offers it to pilgrims who pray for the sick.
Make a pilgrimage to Saint Joseph's Oratory in Montreal, in person or online through the shrine's website.
Pray for vocations to religious life, especially for religious brothers.

andr-bessette.confirmationNote: André can suit a confirmand who serves quietly or feels overlooked. He took the name André when he entered the Congregation of Holy Cross and then spent almost forty years at a college door, turning an ordinary job into a ministry of welcome and prayer. Choosing him is a promise to treat each person who comes to you as someone Christ has sent, and to point others toward St. Joseph and toward God.

This week, visit or help one person who is sick, elderly or homebound, and pray for them by name each day.
Read Genesis 41:53–57 and Matthew 1:18–25, then consider why devotion to St. Joseph borrows Pharaoh's words, 'Go to Joseph.'

biography: no disagreement with the reviewed biography. The Oratory adds birth on August 9, 1845, at Saint-Grégoire d'Iberville; entry into the Holy Cross novitiate December 27, 1870; the chapel blessed October 19, 1904; beatification May 23, 1982; and about a million people at his funeral

andrew.heroSummary: St. Andrew the Apostle was a fisherman from Bethsaida, a disciple of John the Baptist and the brother of Simon Peter, whom he brought to Jesus. Byzantine tradition calls him the "First-Called." The Church celebrates him on November 30, and later tradition holds that he was martyred at Patras on an X-shaped cross.
andrew.searchDescription: St. Andrew the Apostle, fisherman of Bethsaida and brother of Peter, brought others to Jesus. Feast: November 30. Tradition links him to Patras.

symbols.meaning: A later tradition, recorded in the sixth-century Passion of Andrew, says he was crucified at Patras on a diagonal cross; the Gospels do not describe his death.
His trade as a fisherman on the Sea of Galilee, and the boy's five loaves and two fishes he pointed out to Jesus (John 6:8–9).
Jesus called him from casting his net to become a fisher of men (Matthew 4:18–20).
His mission as an apostle sent to carry the Gospel.

andrew.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Andrew when they want to share their faith but do not know how to begin. The Gospels never give him a long speech. Instead they show him following Jesus after John the Baptist pointed him out, then going straight to find his brother with the news that they had found the Messiah. Later he noticed a boy with five loaves and two fish, and he helped some Greeks who wanted to see Jesus. Tradition holds that he preached around the Black Sea and in Greece and died on a cross at Patras. Asking his help is a way of learning to bring others to Christ, one person at a time.

quotes.text: He findeth first his brother Simon, and saith to him: We have found the Messias, which is, being interpreted, the Christ. And he brought him to Jesus.

And Jesus walking by the sea of Galilee, saw two brethren, Simon who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea (for they were fishers). And he saith to them: Come ye after me, and I will make you to be fishers of men. And they immediately leaving their nets, followed him.
One of his disciples, Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter, saith to him: There is a boy here that hath five barley loaves, and two fishes; but what are these among so many?

prayer.text: Hail and blessed be the hour and moment in which the Son of God was born of the most pure Virgin Mary, at midnight, in Bethlehem, in piercing cold. In that hour vouchsafe, O my God! to hear my prayer and grant my desires, [here mention your request] through the merits of Our Saviour Jesus Christ, and of His blessed Mother. Amen.
prayer.source: St. Andrew Christmas Novena, text as given by Catholic Culture (Liturgical Year, November 30)
prayer.note: Traditionally prayed fifteen times a day from the feast of St. Andrew until Christmas. It takes its name from the day it begins; it is addressed to God, not to St. Andrew, and is not attributed to him. Its exact origin is not documented in the sources consulted.

link.label: St. Andrew Christmas Novena at Catholic Culture

feastCustoms: Attend Mass on November 30, the feast of St. Andrew, Apostle, in the Roman calendar.
Begin the St. Andrew Christmas Novena on his feast and pray it each day until Christmas as a way into Advent.

Pray for Christian unity. St. Andrew is patron of the Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople, and for decades the Holy See has sent a delegation to the Patriarchate's November 30 celebration, while the Patriarchate sends one to Rome for Sts. Peter and Paul.
In Scotland, whose flag carries his saltire, November 30 is St. Andrew's Day; Catholics can pray at the shrine holding two of his relics in St. Mary's Cathedral, Edinburgh.
Follow Andrew's example by inviting one person to Mass, to a parish event or to a conversation about Jesus.

andrew.confirmationNote: Andrew suits a confirmand who wants to share faith through friendship rather than argument. In John's Gospel he hears about Jesus, spends a day with him and then goes to find his own brother. Confirmation strengthens the baptized to bear witness to Christ, and Andrew shows how that witness often begins: with a simple invitation to someone close. Choosing him is a promise to help others meet Jesus.
reflectionPrompts: Who first brought you to Jesus, and who might God be asking you to bring to him?
Invite one friend or family member to Mass, a parish event or a conversation about faith this week.
Read John 1:35–42, John 6:5–13 and John 12:20–22, and note what Andrew does in each scene.

andrew-corsini.heroSummary: St. Andrew Corsini was a Florentine Carmelite friar who became bishop of Fiesole in 1349. Remembered for serving the sick during the plague, caring for the poor, insisting on well-prepared priests, and working to make peace between rival cities, he died in 1374. The Carmelites keep his feast on January 9.
andrew-corsini.searchDescription: St. Andrew Corsini, Florentine Carmelite and bishop of Fiesole (1349–1374), remembered for charity, care for priests and peacemaking. Feast: January 9.

symbols.meaning: Tradition: the wild young man who became gentle after turning to God. The Carmelite Order notes he is usually shown with a wolf, a lamb, or both, from a legend that Mary turned a threatening wolf into a lamb; another telling links it to his mother's dream before his birth.
His life as a friar of the Carmelite convent in Florence, which he kept living even as bishop.
His 24 years as bishop of Fiesole, where he visited parishes, examined clergy and cared for the poor.
Tradition says Mary appeared to him at his first Mass and urged him to accept the office of bishop; the scene is carved in G. B. Foggini's relief in the Corsini Chapel in Florence.

andrew-corsini.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Andrew Corsini because his story begins with a change of heart. Tradition holds that he was a worldly young man until his mother's warnings turned him toward the Carmelites in Florence, a turn later pictured as a wolf becoming a lamb. What is documented is the life that followed: he served the sick in the plague of 1348, lived simply as bishop of Fiesole, gave bread and clothing to the needy, insisted on well-formed priests, and worked to settle quarrels between cities. Parents praying for a wandering child, priests, and anyone trying to make peace find in him a patient friend.

quotes.text: Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called children of God.
I say to you, that even so there shall be joy in heaven upon one sinner that doth penance, more than upon ninety-nine just who need not penance.

prayer.text: Lord God, you called Saint Andrew Corsini from a careless youth into the Carmelite life and made him a shepherd for the people of Fiesole. Through his prayers, turn my heart wherever it has wandered, and give patience to every parent who waits for a child to come home. Make our bishops and priests generous and well prepared, and give us courage to make peace where there is quarrel. Teach me to share my bread with the poor as he did, and to serve the sick without fear. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

link.label: Saint Andrew Corsini and a Carmelite collect (British Province of Carmelites)

feastCustoms: Keep his feast on January 9, the date on which the Carmelite Order celebrates him. He died on the evening of the Epiphany in 1374, and the older Roman calendar (1962 Missal) assigns him February 4.
Pray for someone who has drifted from the faith, remembering the tradition that his own mother's urging turned him toward God.
Bring food or clothing to a parish pantry or shelter; the Carmelite account recalls that he gave out bread at his door and grain and clothing to the needy.
Pray for your bishop, priests and seminarians, in honor of his care for well-formed clergy.
Take one concrete step toward reconciliation in a family, parish or workplace quarrel; the Holy See sent him to Bologna in 1368 to settle serious disputes.

andrew-corsini.confirmationNote: St. Andrew Corsini can suit a Confirmation candidate who knows what it is to change direction. Tradition remembers a careless youth who turned toward God, and history remembers the bishop he became: generous to the poor, serious about forming good priests, and willing to step into conflicts to make peace. Taking his name can mean committing to conversion, charity and reconciliation in everyday life.
reflectionPrompts: Is there an area of your life that needs the kind of change of heart tradition attributes to the young Andrew? What would the first step be?
Choose one quarrel near you, in your family, class or workplace, and do one thing this week to help bring peace.
Read Luke 15:1–10, then read the Dicastery for the Causes of Saints' account of Andrea Corsini and note how his work as bishop put conversion into practice.

andrew-dung-lac.heroSummary: St. Andrew Dũng Lạc was a Vietnamese parish priest who learned the faith from a catechist in Hanoi. Ransomed once by his parishioners, he was arrested again and beheaded in Hanoi on December 21, 1839, with Fr. Peter Thi. The Church honors him and 116 fellow martyrs of Vietnam on November 24.
andrew-dung-lac.searchDescription: St. Andrew Dũng Lạc, Vietnamese priest ransomed by his parishioners and beheaded in Hanoi in 1839, honored with 116 fellow martyrs on November 24.
andrew-dung-lac.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Andrew Dũng Lạc because his story is about a whole community keeping faith together. He first came to know Christ through a catechist who gave him a home, and as a priest he depended on parishioners who sheltered him and gathered money to free him after his first arrest. Rather than abandon them, he changed his name and kept serving. The Church remembers him with 116 companions, bishops, priests and many lay men and women, so Vietnamese Catholics and anyone pressured for their faith find in him a sign that no believer stands alone. His last arrest came while he was visiting a brother priest for confession.

quotes.text: Who then shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall tribulation? or distress? or famine? or nakedness? or danger? or persecution? or the sword? ... But in all these things we overcome, because of him that hath loved us.
Remember my word that I said to you: The servant is not greater than his master. If they have persecuted me, they will also persecute you: if they have kept my word, they will keep yours also.

prayer.text: Lord Jesus, you gave Saint Andrew Dũng Lạc a heart for your people and the courage to keep serving them when serving was dangerous. Thank you for the catechists, families and parishioners who sheltered him and paid for his freedom. Through his prayers and those of all the martyrs of Vietnam, strengthen Christians who are pressured to deny you today. Bless catechists and all who teach the faith to the young. When fear tempts me to hide, help me stay faithful, and remind me that I belong to a community of believers. Amen.

feastCustoms: Attend Mass on November 24, the memorial of St. Andrew Dũng Lạc and Companions in the General Roman Calendar, which honors all 117 martyrs of Vietnam canonized together in 1988.
Remember his own death anniversary on December 21, when he and Fr. Peter Thi were beheaded in Hanoi in 1839.
Pray a rosary for Christians who face persecution in Vietnam and elsewhere, as Catholic Culture suggests for this memorial.
Thank or support a catechist in your parish; Andrew first learned the faith from a catechist who took him in.
Share a Vietnamese meal with family or friends, a custom Catholic Culture suggests for November 24.
andrew-dung-lac.confirmationNote: St. Andrew Dũng Lạc can suit a Confirmation candidate who wants a saint of courage rooted in community, or who has Vietnamese roots. He came to faith through a catechist's kindness, served as a parish priest under persecution, and was once freed by his own parishioners before his martyrdom in 1839. Taking his name can mean committing to steady faith and to standing by fellow believers.
reflectionPrompts: Who first taught you the faith or made room for it in your life? How could you thank them this week?
Find out how your parish supports its catechists or persecuted Christians abroad, and offer one concrete form of help this month.
Read Romans 8:31–39, then read Vatican News's account of St. Andrew Dũng Lạc and his companions and note how the community around him made his ministry possible.

andrew-kim-taegon.heroSummary: St. Andrew Kim Taegon was the first Korean-born Catholic priest. Trained in Macau and ordained in Shanghai, he returned home to serve believers under persecution and was beheaded in Seoul on September 16, 1846, in his mid-twenties. Catholics honor him with St. Paul Chong Hasang and their companions on September 20.
andrew-kim-taegon.searchDescription: St. Andrew Kim Taegon, Korea's first native-born priest, ordained in Shanghai and martyred in Seoul in 1846. Honored with his companions on September 20.

symbols.symbol: Traditional Korean dress: a scholar's robe (dopo) and hat
symbols.meaning: His identity as a son of Korea; the marble statue blessed at St. Peter's Basilica in 2023 shows him in this dress, with arms outstretched.

andrew-kim-taegon.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Andrew Kim Taegon because he carried the faith of a persecuted family into the priesthood. His father and grandfather died for Christ, and as a teenager he left home on a long journey to study in Macau. Ordained in Shanghai, he came back to bring the sacraments to Korean believers whose Church had been founded and sustained largely by lay people, and within about a year he was arrested and killed. Seminarians, priests, Korean Catholics, and young people weighing a costly calling find in him a friend who said yes knowing the risk, and who did not shrink from danger.

quotes.text: Every one therefore that shall confess me before men, I will also confess him before my Father who is in heaven.
And how shall they preach unless they be sent, as it is written: How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, of them that bring glad tidings of good things!

prayer.text: Lord Jesus, you called Saint Andrew Kim Taegon from a family of martyrs to be the first priest of his people. Through his prayers, bless the Church in Korea and all who carry the faith where it is costly. Raise up generous priests, and support seminarians who leave home to answer your call. Give peace to the Korean peninsula and to every divided land. When I am afraid to confess you before others, give me his courage, and help me to honor the dignity you have given every person. Amen.

feastCustoms: Attend Mass on September 20, the memorial of Sts. Andrew Kim Taegon, Paul Chong Hasang and Companions, which honors the 103 Korean martyrs canonized in 1984; when September 20 falls on a Sunday, the Sunday liturgy takes its place.
Remember September 16, the anniversary of his martyrdom in 1846.
Pray for seminarians, especially those who must study far from home, as he did in Macau.
Pray for peace on the Korean peninsula, an intention Pope Francis entrusted to his intercession in 2023.
Learn how the Church in Korea began through lay believers, as St. John Paul II described in his 1984 canonization homily.

Taking his name can mean committing to follow God's call when it is costly and to honor the dignity of every person.
reflectionPrompts: What would you be willing to leave behind to follow God's call? What holds you back?
Pray this week for one priest or seminarian by name, and let him know you are praying for him.

angela-merici.heroSummary: St. Angela Merici (1474–1540) grew up near Lake Garda, became a Franciscan tertiary, and in Brescia founded the Company of St. Ursula in 1535: a way for women to consecrate their lives to God while living in the world rather than in a cloister. Canonized in 1807, she is remembered on January 27.
angela-merici.searchDescription: St. Angela Merici, feast January 27, founded the Company of St. Ursula in Brescia in 1535 so women could consecrate their lives to God in the world.

symbols.symbol: Ladder (often with young women climbing it)
symbols.meaning: Tradition recalls a vision in which Angela saw a procession of angels and virgins and heard her late sister tell her she would found a company of virgins; later art shows this as a ladder joining earth and heaven, the path her daughters would climb.

Catholic Culture lists a cloak among her traditional attributes; no reliable source found explains its origin, so it is best treated as an identifying attribute in her images rather than given a fixed meaning.

angela-merici.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Angela Merici when they want to give their whole lives to God without leaving ordinary life behind. She lost her parents and her sister young, prayed through that grief, and spent years joining manual work, prayer and quiet help to neighbors. In Brescia she gathered women who were neither nuns nor wives into a company consecrated to Christ in the middle of the city. Her writings ask leaders to know each person by name and to guide with gentleness, never by force. Women discerning a vocation, teachers, mentors, and anyone carrying responsibility for others find in her a wise, motherly friend.

quotes.text: And the unmarried woman and the virgin thinketh on the things of the Lord, that she may be holy both in body and in spirit.

prayer.text: Lord God, you led St. Angela Merici through loss and long waiting to the work you had prepared for her, and you gave her a mother's heart for the women who followed her. Through her prayers, help me to hear your call in the middle of my ordinary days. Teach me to know the people in my care by name, to guide them with gentleness and never by force, and to trust that you are faithful to what you begin. May I belong wholly to Christ wherever you place me. Amen.

feastCustoms: Attend Mass on January 27, when the General Roman Calendar keeps an optional memorial of St. Angela Merici, Virgin; Ursuline schools and communities often celebrate it more solemnly.
Read part of her Counsels or Testament, which the Ursulines of the Roman Union publish in English alongside the Italian originals.
Pray by name for each person in your care (family, students, team or parishioners), as she urged the leaders of her company to remember each of their daughters by name.
Learn about the Company of St. Ursula, which continues today as a secular institute of women consecrated to God while living in the world.
Thank a woman who has mentored you in faith, or give some time to encouraging a girl or young woman in your parish or community.

angela-merici.confirmationNote: Angela Merici suits a confirmand who wants to belong completely to God without leaving everyday life, and who cares about friendship, mentoring and helping others grow. She waited years before her vocation became clear, and she trusted God through grief and illness. Confirmation strengthens Christians to live their faith in the world, and Angela shows that a consecrated heart can do that in the middle of an ordinary city.
reflectionPrompts: Where in my everyday life is God asking me to belong to him more completely?
Write down the names of the people who depend on you this week and pray for each one by name.
Read St. Angela's Testament on the Ursulines of the Roman Union site and note what she asks of those who lead others.

anicetus.heroSummary: St. Anicetus was a second-century bishop of Rome, originally from Syria. He is remembered for his meeting with St. Polycarp of Smyrna: they disagreed over when to celebrate Easter and neither persuaded the other, yet St. Irenaeus records that they shared the Eucharist and parted in peace. Vatican News commemorates him on April 20.
anicetus.searchDescription: St. Anicetus, a second-century bishop of Rome from Syria, disagreed with Polycarp over the date of Easter, yet the two shared the Eucharist and parted in peace.
anicetus.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Anicetus when a disagreement threatens to become a break. Almost all we know of him comes from one encounter that St. Irenaeus later recalled: the aged Polycarp came to Rome, the two bishops could not agree on how to keep Easter, and still they remained in communion, Anicetus gave Polycarp the honor of celebrating the Eucharist, and they parted as brothers. He is a fitting companion for families, parishes and friends who must live with real differences, and for anyone praying for Christian unity. His example suggests that holding firmly to what we have received and treating others with deep respect can belong together.

quotes.text: But though matters were in this shape, they communed together, and Anicetus conceded the administration of the eucharist in the church to Polycarp, manifestly as a mark of respect. And they parted from each other in peace, both those who observed, and those who did not, maintaining the peace of the whole church.
quotes.work: Irenaeus, letter to Pope Victor, quoted in Eusebius, Church History, Book V, chapter 24, §17
quotes.translation: Arthur Cushman McGiffert, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 1 (1890; public domain)

quotes.text: With all humility and mildness, with patience, supporting one another in charity. Careful to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.

prayer.text: Lord God, St. Anicetus and St. Polycarp could not agree, yet they would not let their disagreement divide your Church. Through the prayers of St. Anicetus, give me the humility to listen, the courage to hold to what is true, and the charity to honor those who see things differently. Heal the divisions among Christians, and gather us one day around a single altar. Where I am quick to quarrel, make me patient; where I am tempted to walk away, teach me to stay at the table. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

feastCustoms: Remember him on April 20, the date under which Vatican News lists him (older references give April 17 or other dates); he is not on the General Roman Calendar, so this is a day for personal or family prayer rather than a Mass in his honor.
Read Eusebius, Church History, Book IV, chapter 14, and Book V, chapter 24, at New Advent, where Irenaeus describes the meeting of Anicetus and Polycarp.
Pray for unity among Christians, especially between Catholic and Orthodox churches, which still often celebrate Easter on different Sundays.
Before a conversation with someone you disagree with, pray Ephesians 4:2–3 and name one thing you honestly respect in them.
Share a meal or a time of prayer with someone whose views differ from yours, as a small sign that disagreement need not end fellowship.
anicetus.confirmationNote: Anicetus suits a confirmand who cares about fairness, peace and keeping people together. He held to the practice he had received at Rome, yet when he could not persuade Polycarp, he honored him and kept communion with him. Confirmation strengthens Christians to witness to Christ, and Anicetus shows that part of that witness is disagreeing with charity, so that the Church's unity is guarded even when opinions differ.
reflectionPrompts: Is there a disagreement in my life that I have let turn into distance, and what would it take to restore peace?
This week, invite someone you disagree with to coffee or a meal and listen more than you speak.
Read Eusebius, Church History, Book V, chapter 24, and note how Irenaeus uses the example of Anicetus and Polycarp to counsel Pope Victor.

anna-wang.heroSummary: St. Anna Wang was a Chinese Catholic girl of fourteen who was killed in 1900, during the Boxer uprising, after refusing to renounce her faith. John Paul II, canonizing her in 2000, recalled that she faced death saying heaven's door is open to all. She is honored among the Martyrs of China.
anna-wang.searchDescription: St. Anna Wang, a 14-year-old Chinese Catholic martyred in 1900, refused to renounce her faith; John Paul II canonized her with the Martyrs of China in 2000.
anna-wang.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Anna Wang because she was so young and so sure. We know little about her daily life, but John Paul II told the world that at fourteen, pressed to give up her faith and facing execution, she would not, and that she went to her death calm, speaking of heaven's open door and murmuring the name of Jesus. She is a natural friend for teenagers who feel pressure to hide or drop their faith, for parents and catechists who form them, and for Christians in China and anywhere believers suffer for Christ. She reminds us that courage does not depend on age.

quotes.text: Every one therefore that shall confess me before men, I will also confess him before my Father who is in heaven.
And fear ye not them that kill the body, and are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him that can destroy both soul and body in hell.

prayer.text: Lord Jesus, St. Anna Wang was only fourteen when she was told to deny you, and she answered with your name on her lips. Through her prayers, give young people the courage to stay faithful when it is hard, and give all of us the peace that does not depend on our circumstances. Strengthen Christians in China and everywhere believers are pressured or persecuted. When I am tempted to hide my faith to fit in, remind me that heaven's door is open and that you are worth everything. Amen.

feastCustoms: Remember her on July 9, when the General Roman Calendar keeps an optional memorial of St. Augustine Zhao Rong and Companions, the martyrs of China among whom she was canonized.
Read the passage about her in John Paul II's homily for the canonization of October 1, 2000, available on the Vatican website.
Pray for Catholics in China and for Christians anywhere who face pressure or violence because of their faith.
With teenagers, talk about times it is hard to admit you are a Christian, and pray Matthew 10:32 together.
Read the L'Osservatore Romano account of the 120 martyrs (reproduced by Catholic Culture) to learn the names of those who died with her generation in 1900.
anna-wang.confirmationNote: Anna Wang suits a confirmand who wants courage to stand by their faith under pressure, especially from people their own age or from those with power. She was fourteen, about the age of many confirmands, when she refused to deny Christ. Confirmation strengthens Christians to confess Christ boldly, and Anna shows that this strength is not reserved for adults or heroes but is offered to the young.
reflectionPrompts: When have I kept quiet about my faith because I was afraid of what others would think?
Choose one simple, visible way to show you are a Christian this week, such as grace before a meal in public.
Read the passage on the martyrs of China in John Paul II's homily of October 1, 2000, and Matthew 10:26–33.

anne.heroSummary: St. Anne is honored as a patron of mothers and, with St. Joachim, of grandparents. Scripture does not name Mary's parents; the name Anne and the story of her long childlessness come from the second-century Protoevangelium of James and later tradition. The Church celebrates Joachim and Anne together on July 26.
anne.searchDescription: St. Anne, honored with St. Joachim on July 26, is by tradition Mary's mother; her name comes from the Protoevangelium of James, not the Gospels.

symbols.symbol: Mary, and often the Child Jesus, in her arms or on her lap
symbols.meaning: Her place in Catholic devotion as mother of Mary and grandmother of Jesus, three generations shown together.

symbols.symbol: Book, often shown as Anne teaching the young Mary to read
symbols.meaning: Her care in forming her daughter in faith; the scene is devotional imagination, not a recorded event.
From the Protoevangelium of James, where childless Anne sees a sparrow's nest in a laurel tree and grieves; it stands for her longing and her answered prayer.
Later tradition, building on the Protoevangelium, places her joyful meeting with Joachim at this gate after angels announce that she will conceive.

anne.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Anne because she stands where so many of us stand: in a family, praying for the people we love. Scripture tells us nothing about her, not even her name; what we have comes from an early noncanonical writing and centuries of devotion. Yet that tradition speaks to real lives: a couple who waited years for a child, a mother who handed on faith to her daughter, a grandmother of Jesus. Mothers, couples longing for children, grandparents and anyone raising young people ask her prayers. Tradition holds that her home was where Mary first learned to pray.

quotes.text: For this child did I pray, and the Lord hath granted me my petition, which I asked of him. Therefore I also have lent him to the Lord all the days of his life...
quotes.work: 1 Kings 1:27–28 (1 Samuel 1:27–28 in modern numbering), the prayer of Hannah, on which the Protoevangelium's story of Anne is closely modeled

quotes.text: And his mercy is from generation unto generations, to them that fear him.

prayer.text: Lord God, the Church has long honored St. Anne as the mother of the Virgin Mary. Through her prayers, bless our families and the generations that came before us. Comfort those who long for a child, strengthen mothers and grandparents in their daily care, and help all who raise children to pass on the faith with patience and love. As Mary learned to trust you at home, let our homes become places where your mercy is known from generation to generation. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

In Brittany, pilgrims gather for the Grand Pardon at Sainte-Anne-d'Auray on July 25 and 26, with a torchlight procession and a solemn Mass.
In France and French Canada, a summer fruit tart is a traditional dish for the day; share one with family.

anne.confirmationNote: Anne suits a confirmand who is grateful for the faith received from parents, grandparents or godparents and wants to hand it on. Nothing she said or did is recorded in Scripture, so choosing her is a choice to honor quiet faithfulness inside a family. Confirmation strengthens Christians to witness to Christ, and that witness often begins at home, in the way we pray with and care for the people closest to us.

ansbert.heroSummary: St. Ansbert (died about 695) left a career at the Frankish royal court to become a monk under St. Wandrille at Fontenelle, where he later served as abbot. In 684 he became bishop of Rouen. Caught up in the politics of his day, he died in exile at Hautmont. His local feast is February 9.
ansbert.searchDescription: St. Ansbert (d. c. 695), feast February 9: royal official turned monk of Fontenelle, abbot, and bishop of Rouen who died in exile at Hautmont.
ansbert.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Ansbert when they are weighing success against something deeper. The records are brief, but they show a man who left honors at the court of Clotaire III to follow Christ as a monk, then accepted the burden of leading an abbey and a diocese. His last years were spent far from home, exiled for political reasons; the monks of Saint-Wandrille say he was a victim of jealousy. He did not get to finish his work on his own terms. Anyone who has been pushed aside unfairly, or who must choose between ambition and conscience, can ask his prayers.

prayer.text: Lord God, you drew St. Ansbert away from the honors of a royal court to seek you in the quiet of the monastery, and you kept him faithful as bishop and as an exile. Through his prayers, free me from the need for status and approval. Help me to serve wherever you place me, to lead without grasping for power, and to forgive those who treat me unjustly. When my plans are cut short, teach me to trust that my life is in your hands. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

feastCustoms: St. Ansbert is not on the universal calendar; the monks of Saint-Wandrille keep his feast on February 9, so remember him in personal prayer that day.
Pray for the Benedictine monks of Saint-Wandrille, who still live at the site of his monastery.
Pray for the Archdiocese of Rouen and its bishop.
Pray for people living in exile or forced from their work for political reasons.
Set aside a period of quiet today, away from screens and status-seeking, in the spirit of his move from court to cloister.

places.name: Abbey of Saint-Wandrille (Fontenelle)

ansbert.confirmationNote: Ansbert suits a confirmand who is generous, gifted at organizing, or wrestling with ambition. He had an influential position at the royal court and gave it up to follow Christ, then used his abilities to serve his monastery and his diocese. When political enemies drove him out, he stayed faithful. Confirmation strengthens Christians to put their talents at God's service, and Ansbert shows how to do that without clinging to status.
reflectionPrompts: What honor or approval do I hold onto too tightly?
Offer one practical act of help this week to someone who has been treated unfairly or pushed out of their place.
Read Matthew 19:27–29 in the Douay-Rheims, St. Peter's question about leaving everything, and consider Ansbert's choice to leave the court.

quotes: omitted. No writings of his survive in a public-domain English translation, and no Scripture passage is specifically tied to him in the sources.

biography: no contradiction, two additions for a human. The Saint-Wandrille monks call him the abbey's third abbot, chosen by Wandrille as one of his immediate successors, and say he became bishop of Rouen in 684 after the death of St. Ouen. They describe him as a 'victim of jealousy'; Nominis names Pepin of Herstal as the ruler who exiled him. The abbey adds that his body was brought back to Fontenelle, later moved to Ghent (Mont-Blandin), and destroyed by Calvinists in 1578. Nominis says he was chancellor at Clotaire III's court and names him also Austrebert.

relatedSaints: Bathildis was regent for Clotaire III in the early part of his reign; the sources do not say whether Ansbert served at court during her regency. Willibrord is linked by era and by Pepin of Herstal, not by any recorded contact.
reflectionPrompts: the Matthew passage is a thematic choice, not one the sources connect to him.

anselm-of-canterbury.heroSummary: St. Anselm of Canterbury (1033–1109) was a Benedictine monk from Aosta who taught and prayed at the abbey of Bec before becoming archbishop of Canterbury in 1093. His Proslogion and Cur Deus Homo explore faith seeking understanding, and his defense of the Church's freedom twice cost him exile. His feast is April 21.
anselm-of-canterbury.searchDescription: St. Anselm of Canterbury (1033–1109), feast April 21: Benedictine abbot of Bec, archbishop, and Doctor of the Church who believed in order to understand.

symbols.meaning: His decades as a monk, prior, and abbot of Bec, where he taught in the cloister school and wrote his first major works.
His office as archbishop of Canterbury from 1093, which he accepted reluctantly and held through long disputes with the crown.
A traditional attribute listed by Catholic Culture; it is commonly read as his sea crossings into exile in defense of the Church, though the origin of the image is not documented.
His tender devotion to the Virgin Mary, which Benedict XVI singled out; the vision scene is a devotional image rather than a documented event.
His writings, above all the Monologion, Proslogion, and Cur Deus Homo, which earned him the title Father of Scholasticism.

anselm-of-canterbury.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Anselm when faith and hard questions arrive together. He did not treat reason as a rival to belief; he prayed his way into thinking, and his most famous argument begins as a conversation with God. Students, teachers, and anyone wrestling with doubt find in him a patient guide. Pastors and leaders remember that he accepted an office he did not want, stood firm when kings pressed on the Church's freedom, and twice went into exile rather than give way. He also loved Mary tenderly. Above all, he shows that the search for God is worth our best attention and our quietest prayer.

quotes.text: Up now, slight man! flee, for a little while, thy occupations; hide thyself, for a time, from thy disturbing thoughts. Cast aside, now, thy burdensome cares, and put away thy toilsome business.
quotes.translation: Sidney Norton Deane (Open Court, 1903), public domain

quotes.text: For I do not seek to understand that I may believe, but I believe in order to understand. For this also I believe,—that unless I believed, I should not understand.
quotes.translation: Sidney Norton Deane (Open Court, 1903), public domain

quotes.text: My heart hath said to thee: My face hath sought thee: thy face, O Lord, will I still seek.
quotes.work: Psalm 26:8 (Psalm 27:8 in modern numbering), which Anselm quotes in Proslogium chapter 1

prayer.text: Teach me to seek thee, and reveal thyself to me, when I seek thee, for I cannot seek thee, except thou teach me, nor find thee, except thou reveal thyself. Let me seek thee in longing, let me long for thee in seeking; let me find thee in love, and love thee in finding.
prayer.source: St. Anselm, Proslogium, chapter 1, translated by Sidney Norton Deane (Open Court, 1903), as given by the Christian Classics Ethereal Library
prayer.note: This is a passage from the prayer that opens the Proslogium, verified word for word against Deane's public-domain translation. Some online versions modernize 'thee' and 'thou'.

link.label: Read the Proslogium (Deane translation) at CCEL

feastCustoms: Attend Mass on April 21, an optional memorial of St. Anselm, bishop and Doctor of the Church, in the General Roman Calendar.
Set aside a quiet quarter of an hour and pray slowly through chapter 1 of the Proslogion, which he wrote as a prayer before it became an argument.
Pray for bishops, pastors, and all who must defend the Church's freedom under pressure, a lesson Pope Benedict XVI drew from Anselm's exiles.
Bring one real question about the faith to a book, a teacher, or a priest, in the spirit of faith seeking understanding.
Honor Mary with a short prayer or rosary decade, recalling the Marian devotion that marked his life.

He prayed and thought at the same time, and he held firm under pressure from powerful people. Choosing his name can mean committing to keep learning the faith honestly and to defend what is right with courage and gentleness.
reflectionPrompts: What question about God or the faith do I carry right now, and have I ever turned it into a prayer rather than keeping it to myself?
Clear fifteen minutes this week with no phone or noise, and spend it in silent prayer, as Anselm urges at the start of the Proslogion.
Read chapter 1 of the Proslogium in Deane's translation, then Psalm 26 (27) in the Douay-Rheims, and note which lines Anselm borrows.

ansgar.heroSummary: St. Ansgar (801–865), called the Apostle of the North, was a Benedictine monk of Corbie who carried the Gospel to Denmark and Sweden. As bishop of Hamburg and later Bremen, he rebuilt after Hamburg was destroyed in 845, ransomed captives and cared for the sick. His disciple Rimbert wrote his Life; his feast is February 3.
ansgar.searchDescription: St. Ansgar (801–865), feast February 3: Benedictine monk and bishop of Hamburg-Bremen, the Apostle of the North who preached in Denmark and Sweden.

symbols.meaning: The Church he planted as first bishop of Hamburg and the small churches he built in Denmark and Sweden.
The clothing of a missionary who traveled through the cold lands of the North.
His office as bishop of Hamburg and later of the united see of Hamburg-Bremen, a shepherd for peoples who had not yet heard the Gospel.

ansgar.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Ansgar when their work for God seems to fail. Rimbert's Life describes missions that collapsed, a city burned, churches abandoned and funding cut off, yet Ansgar kept starting again. He built hospitals, ransomed captives, pressed a Danish king to ease the slave trade and gave generously to the poor. When people praised his miracles, he answered that the only miracle he wanted was to be made a good man. Missionaries, people serving in hard places and anyone tempted to measure faithfulness by quick results find in him a patient, humble companion.

quotes.text: Were I worthy of such a favour from my God, I would ask that he would grant to me this one miracle, that by His grace He would make of me a good man.
quotes.work: Rimbert, Life of Anskar, chapter 39 (Ansgar's words to a friend, as reported by his disciple)
quotes.translation: Charles H. Robinson, Anskar, the Apostle of the North (London: SPCK, 1921; public domain)

quotes.text: Into thy hands I commend my spirit: thou hast redeemed me, O Lord, the God of truth.
quotes.work: Psalm 30:6 (Psalm 31:6 in modern numbering), among the verses Rimbert says Ansgar repeated as he died

prayer.text: Lord God, you sent St. Ansgar to peoples who did not yet know you, and you kept him faithful when his work was undone again and again. Through his prayers, give me patience when my efforts seem to come to nothing, and courage to begin again. Make me generous to the poor, attentive to the sick, and ready to work for the freedom of those who are bound. Bless all who carry the Gospel to hard places today. And, as Ansgar asked, grant me the one miracle that matters most: by your grace, make me a good person. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

feastCustoms: St. Ansgar has an optional memorial in the universal Roman calendar on February 3; ask whether your parish will celebrate it at Mass.
February 3 is also the memorial of St. Blaise, so many parishes offer the blessing of throats that day; pray for Ansgar's intercession alongside it.
In Denmark, Sweden and northern Germany, where he is honored as patron, remember the Catholic communities of Scandinavia in prayer.
Support a missionary or a charity that frees captives or victims of human trafficking, recalling his work to ransom captives.
Read a few chapters of Rimbert's Life of Anskar, especially chapters 39–41 on his humility and death.

ansgar.confirmationNote: Ansgar suits a confirmand who is brave, persistent, or drawn to mission. He traveled into unfamiliar and dangerous places to share the Gospel, saw much of his work destroyed, and still kept going without bitterness. He also cared for prisoners, the sick and the poor. Confirmation strengthens Christians to witness to Christ wherever they are sent, and Ansgar shows that faithful perseverance is itself a form of courage.
reflectionPrompts: Where have I given up on something good because the results came slowly?
Choose one concrete act this week for someone who is not free, such as a prisoner, a migrant or a victim of trafficking.

anthony-mary-claret.heroSummary: St. Anthony Mary Claret was a Catalan weaver turned missionary preacher who founded the Claretians in 1849, served as archbishop of Santiago de Cuba, and spread the faith through cheap books and pamphlets. He survived an assassin's razor and forgave his attacker. His feast is October 24.
anthony-mary-claret.searchDescription: St. Anthony Mary Claret (1807–1870), feast October 24: Catalan missionary, founder of the Claretians, and archbishop of Santiago de Cuba.

symbols.meaning: His service as archbishop of Santiago de Cuba from 1850, during which he made three pastoral visitations of his diocese.
His preaching and his publishing apostolate: he founded the Religious Library in 1848 and wrote a great many books and pamphlets for ordinary readers.
His Marian devotion, which gave his congregation its name: Missionary Sons of the Immaculate Heart of Mary.
"The charity of Christ presseth us" (2 Corinthians 5:14), the motto he placed on his episcopal coat of arms.

anthony-mary-claret.whyWeTurn: Claret never stopped moving. He preached in villages across Catalonia and the Canary Islands, made three pastoral visitations of his diocese in Cuba, and when he could not be present, he sent books and leaflets in his place. People turn to him when they want to share their faith in practical ways, when they work with words, print, or media, or when they feel worn down by opposition. His most striking lesson came at Holguín in 1856: slashed across the face by a would-be assassin, he forgave the man and pleaded for his pardon. He shows that zeal and mercy can live in the same heart.

quotes.text: For the charity of Christ presseth us: judging this, that if one died for all, then all were dead.

prayer.text: Lord Jesus, your love urged St. Anthony Mary Claret to carry the Gospel to towns, islands, and cities, by voice and by the printed word. Set my heart on fire with that same love. Give me courage to speak of you plainly and kindly, and creativity to share your truth with people who would never hear a sermon. When I am opposed or hurt, help me to forgive as he forgave the man who tried to kill him. Through the prayers of Mary's Immaculate Heart, make me a missionary wherever I am. Amen.

feastCustoms: October 24 is his optional memorial in the General Roman Calendar; attend Mass or pray the day's collect, which asks for his zeal in winning others for Christ.
Claretian parishes, schools, and communities around the world celebrate the day as the feast of their founder.
Give or share a good Catholic book, or support a Catholic publisher or magazine, continuing his press apostolate.
Pray by name for someone who has hurt you, remembering how he forgave his attacker at Holguín.
Pray for the Church in Cuba and in the Canary Islands, where he preached and served.

anthony-mary-claret.confirmationNote: Claret suits a candidate who is energetic, practical, and eager to share the faith, perhaps through writing, speaking, design, or media. He learned a trade first, then gave every skill to the Gospel, and he forgave someone who tried to kill him. Choosing him can be a commitment to use your talents for others and to answer hostility with mercy.
reflectionPrompts: Who in my life is hard for me to forgive, and what would one small step toward mercy look like this week?
Find one practical way to share something good about your faith this week: a book, a message, or an invitation.

anthony-mary-zaccaria.heroSummary: St. Anthony Mary Zaccaria (1502–1539) was a doctor from Cremona who became a priest and a reformer in Milan. Inspired by St. Paul, he founded the Barnabites, the Angelic Sisters and a community of married laypeople, and promoted Eucharistic adoration and devotion to the Crucified. He died at about 36; his feast is July 5.
anthony-mary-zaccaria.searchDescription: St. Anthony Mary Zaccaria (1502–1539), feast July 5: doctor turned priest who founded the Barnabites and Angelic Sisters in the spirit of St. Paul.

symbols.meaning: Christ crucified was the center of his preaching; the Barnabites recall that he preached in Milan's streets with a crucifix in hand.
His love for the Eucharist, frequent Communion and public adoration, which the Barnabites associate with the early Forty Hours devotion in Milan.
Purity of heart; his relics in Milan are shown holding a silver lily.
The Apostle whose spirit shaped his three foundations, all named for St. Paul.
The simple clerical dress of the Clerics Regular of St. Paul he founded.

anthony-mary-zaccaria.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Anthony Mary Zaccaria when their faith has grown lukewarm and they want it to burn again. He was a trained physician who decided he was called to heal souls, and he kept caring for the sick as a priest. He gathered priests, religious women and married couples into one shared mission of renewal, drawing on St. Paul's urgency and love for Christ crucified. Doctors, nurses, students of medicine, and anyone who wants to live their ordinary work as a vocation find in him an energetic, practical guide. The Barnabites still honor him as patron of physicians.

quotes.text: But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ; by whom the world is crucified to me, and I to the world.
quotes.work: Galatians 6:14 (St. Paul, whose spirituality of the Cross shaped Zaccaria's foundations)

quotes.text: Furthermore I count all things to be but loss for the excellent knowledge of Jesus Christ my Lord...
quotes.work: Philippians 3:8 (echoed in the collect for his memorial)

prayer.text: Lord Jesus, you called St. Anthony Mary Zaccaria from healing bodies to healing souls, and filled him with St. Paul's love for your Cross. Through his prayers, wake me from lukewarm habits and set my heart on fire for you. Help me to find you in the Eucharist, to look often at the crucifix, and to see my daily work as a way of serving others. Bless doctors, nurses and all who care for the sick. Make me eager to grow in the knowledge of you, and generous in sharing it. Amen.

anthony-mary-zaccaria.confirmationNote: Anthony Mary Zaccaria suits a confirmand who is joyful, energetic, or thinking about a career in medicine or service. He used his medical training to care for people's bodies and then gave his life to renewing their faith. He drew laypeople, priests and religious women into a common mission. Confirmation sends Christians out to share the Spirit's fire with others, and he shows how to do that with enthusiasm and love for the Cross.

anthony-of-padua.heroSummary: St. Anthony of Padua was a Portuguese Franciscan preacher and Doctor of the Church, known in popular devotion as the saint who helps people find what they have lost. Born Fernando in Lisbon, he died near Padua on June 13, 1231, the date of his feast. His sermons matter as much as his miracles.
anthony-of-padua.searchDescription: St. Anthony of Padua (c. 1195–1231) was a Franciscan preacher and Doctor of the Church. Learn about his life, June 13 feast, and help with lost things.

symbols.symbol: The Child Jesus in his arms
symbols.meaning: Recalls a vision of the Christ Child reported at Camposampiero near the end of his life (tradition), and his love for the humanity of Christ.
Purity of heart and his lifelong struggle against evil; pilgrims still bring lilies to his tomb in Padua.
His knowledge of Scripture, his teaching of theology, and his preaching; he is honored as a Doctor of the Church.
Charity toward the poor, continued in the devotion called St. Anthony's Bread.
His choice, in 1220, to leave the Augustinian canons and become a Friar Minor.

anthony-of-padua.whyWeTurn: Most people meet St. Anthony while hunting for keys or a lost ring. A Franciscan account traces the habit to a borrowed psalter that a novice took and later returned after Anthony prayed; legend embellished the story, but the core is likely true. That small, everyday help is real comfort, and it can lead further. Anthony was first a preacher who spent himself on the crowds of Padua, heard confessions for hours, and confronted greed that crushed the poor. When we turn to him, we can ask him to help us find what we have misplaced, and also what matters more: peace with God, a way back to the sacraments, or a neighbor's need we have overlooked.

quotes.text: Preach the word: be instant in season, out of season: reprove, entreat, rebuke in all patience and doctrine.

Or what woman having ten groats; if she lose one groat, doth not light a candle, and sweep the house, and seek diligently until she find it? And when she hath found it, call together her friends and neighbours, saying: Rejoice with me, because I have found the groat which I had lost.

prayer.text: Lord God, you gave St. Anthony a love for your Word and a heart for those who were lost or poor. Through his prayers, help me to search patiently for what I have misplaced, and to trust you when it stays hidden. Find me, too, where I have wandered from you, and bring me home through the mercy of your sacraments. Make me generous to people in need, so that whatever I receive becomes bread for someone else. Give me Anthony's courage to speak the truth with charity. Amen.

anthony-the-great.heroSummary: St. Anthony the Great (about 250–356) is a patron of farmers and is invoked as a protector of animals. An Egyptian Christian, he gave away his inheritance after hearing the Gospel and spent most of his life in the desert. The Life attributed to St. Athanasius spread his example widely, and his memorial is January 17.
anthony-the-great.searchDescription: St. Anthony the Great (c. 250–356), feast January 17: Egyptian desert hermit, father of monks, patron of farmers and protector of animals.

symbols.meaning: The hermit's staff in the form of the Greek and Hebrew letter tau, a sign of the cross and of his long life as a desert monk.

symbols.symbol: Pig, often with a bell at its neck
symbols.meaning: Linked to the medieval Antonine hospitallers, who raised pigs because their fat was used to anoint the sick; it later made him a protector of farm animals.
Hung from his tau staff or at the pig's neck in many images; Catholic Culture lists the bell among his attributes, and he is a patron of bell ringers.
The painful disease ergotism was called "St. Anthony's fire," and the sick sought his intercession at Antonine hospitals.
The Scriptures he carried in memory; the Life says he listened so closely that his memory served him for books.

anthony-the-great.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Anthony when they need courage in spiritual struggle. The Life attributed to Athanasius shows him as a man who heard one line of the Gospel and took it literally, then spent decades learning to pray, work with his hands and resist temptation. Yet the portrait is not grim: early writers remember his cheerfulness, his gentleness with visitors and his advice that good judgment matters more than heroic effort. Farmers and anyone who keeps animals have long asked his protection, a custom tradition holds grew from the hospitals that bore his name. He reminds us that peace with God is built one faithful day at a time.

quotes.text: Wherefore fear them not, but rather ever breathe Christ, and trust Him. Live as though dying daily.
quotes.work: Athanasius, Life of Antony, section 91 (Antony's farewell counsel to his disciples, about the demons)
quotes.translation: H. Ellershaw, in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 4 (1892; public domain)

quotes.text: For it is not far from us, nor is it without ourselves, but it is within us, and is easy if only we are willing.
quotes.work: Athanasius, Life of Antony, section 20 (Antony speaking of virtue to the monks)
quotes.translation: H. Ellershaw, in Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 4 (1892; public domain)

quotes.text: Jesus saith to him: If thou wilt be perfect, go sell what thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come follow me.
quotes.work: Matthew 19:21 (the Gospel Anthony heard in church before giving away his inheritance)

prayer.text: Lord Jesus Christ, you called St. Anthony through a single verse of your Gospel, and he followed you into the desert with an undivided heart. Through his prayers, help me to hear your word as if it were spoken to me today. When I am tempted or afraid, teach me to breathe your name and trust you. Give me patience in ordinary work, gentleness with those who seek me out, and the good judgment he prized above every hard practice. Watch over farmers, their land and their animals. And bring us all to the treasure in heaven you promised to those who follow you. Amen.

feastCustoms: Join the Church's universal memorial of St. Anthony, Abbot, at Mass on January 17.
In Italy and many rural places, stables and domestic animals are blessed on his feast; ask whether a nearby parish offers a blessing of animals.
Read the opening sections of the Life of Antony, especially his response to Matthew 19:21, in the public-domain Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers translation.
Pray for monks, nuns and hermits, and for vocations to monastic life.
Give something away today that you have been holding onto, as Anthony gave his inheritance to his neighbors and the poor.
anthony-the-great.confirmationNote: Anthony suits a confirmand who wants to take the Gospel seriously and is ready for spiritual effort. He heard one verse at Mass and acted on it, then spent years learning prayer, work and self-control. The Life presents his struggles with temptation honestly, but always ends with trust in Christ. Confirmation strengthens Christians for that same struggle, and Anthony shows that steady faithfulness matters more than dramatic gestures.
reflectionPrompts: Which line of the Gospel do I already know is meant for me, and what keeps me from acting on it?
Choose one possession, habit or distraction to give up this week, and use the time you gain to pray.

apollinaris.heroSummary: St. Apollinaris is honored as the first bishop of Ravenna and as a martyr, and the city still counts him as its patron. Tradition links him to Antioch and to St. Peter, but his dates are uncertain. His memory shines in the sixth-century Basilica of Sant'Apollinare in Classe, and the Church remembers him on July 20.
apollinaris.searchDescription: St. Apollinaris, feast July 20: honored as Ravenna's first bishop and a martyr, remembered in the great basilica of Sant'Apollinare in Classe.

symbols.meaning: In the sixth-century apse mosaic at Classe he stands with open arms in the ancient posture of prayer, interceding for his people. It is the earliest and most famous image of him.
The lambs around him in the Classe mosaic stand for the faithful he shepherded as Ravenna's first bishop.

symbols.symbol: White vestments marked with black crosses
symbols.meaning: The white stole or pallium of a bishop, worn over a chasuble in the mosaic; it marks him as the founding pastor of the Church of Ravenna.
Tradition says he was beaten repeatedly for his preaching and died of his injuries.
From the later legend of his sufferings, which tells of repeated tortures; it is not part of the early evidence for his life.

apollinaris.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Apollinaris when they think about the beginnings of faith in a place: who first brought the Gospel to their town, and what it cost. Ravenna has remembered him as its first bishop for many centuries, and when its Christians built their greatest church at Classe, they put him, not Christ enthroned, in the center of the apse, praying with open arms over his flock. Tradition holds that he was beaten again and again for preaching and kept returning to his people. He is a good companion for bishops, priests and anyone who has been sent somewhere new to build up a community of faith.

quotes.text: Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking care of it, not by constraint, but willingly, according to God: not for filthy lucre's sake, but voluntarily: Neither as lording it over the clergy, but being made a pattern of the flock from the heart.
And when the prince of pastors shall appear, you shall receive a never fading crown of glory.
And he was transfigured before them. And his face did shine as the sun: and his garments became white as snow.
quotes.work: Matthew 17:2 (the Transfiguration, shown symbolically above him in the apse at Classe)

prayer.text: Lord God, you gave the Church of Ravenna St. Apollinaris as its first shepherd, who would not stop preaching your Gospel even when he was beaten for it. Through his prayers, bless our bishop and our priests with courage and a shepherd's heart. Help us to cherish the faith that others carried to us at great cost, and to hand it on with love to those who come after us. Like the people of Ravenna, may we keep our eyes on Christ, whose glory shone on the mountain. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

feastCustoms: Attend Mass on July 20, when St. Apollinaris may be celebrated as an optional memorial in the General Roman Calendar; Catholic Culture notes this memorial was restored in 2002.
In Classe, near Ravenna, the local celebration is kept on July 23, his older feast day.
Look closely at a photograph of the apse mosaic at Sant'Apollinare in Classe and pray with him in the orans posture he is shown in.
Read 1 Peter 5:1–4 and pray for your own bishop by name.
Find out who first brought the faith to your diocese or parish, and thank God for them.

Ravenna remembers him as the pastor who first gathered its Christian community and kept preaching despite beatings. Confirmation sends Christians out to bear witness, and Apollinaris is a patron for those who are sent.

apollonia.heroSummary: St. Apollonia was an elderly Christian woman of Alexandria who died in mob violence against Christians shortly before the persecution of Decius, about 249. Her bishop, Dionysius, described her death in a letter that Eusebius preserved. Because her teeth were broken, Catholics have long invoked her against toothache. Her memory is kept on February 9.
apollonia.searchDescription: St. Apollonia, feast February 9: an elderly Christian of Alexandria killed by a mob about 249, invoked against toothache because her teeth were broken.

symbols.meaning: Her best-known attribute. Dionysius says the mob broke out all her teeth; later art turned this into pincers, which is why people with toothache ask her prayers.

symbols.symbol: A single tooth, sometimes gilded or worn on a chain
symbols.meaning: A shorthand for the same injury, used when the pincers are left out.
The common sign of a martyr's victory; artists often pair it with her tooth.
The fire the crowd lit outside the city. Dionysius says that, released for a moment, she went into it herself rather than repeat their blasphemies.

apollonia.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Apollonia most often in very ordinary pain: a toothache, a dreaded dental appointment, a child's sore jaw. Because a mob broke her teeth, tradition holds that she understands that kind of suffering, and dentists have long counted her as their patron. But her story is about more than teeth. She was an old woman, respected in her community, who stayed faithful when a crowd demanded that she join their blasphemies. Catholic Culture suggests asking her prayers for a courageous and holy death, and older Catholics may find in her a friend who knows that age does not end our witness.

quotes.text: Then they seized also that most admirable virgin, Apollonia, an old woman, and, smiting her on the jaws, broke out all her teeth.
quotes.work: Dionysius of Alexandria, Letter to Fabius of Antioch, quoted in Eusebius, Church History VI.41.7 (Dionysius writing about Apollonia)
quotes.translation: Arthur Cushman McGiffert, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series, vol. 1 (1890), public domain

quotes.text: And they made a fire outside the city and threatened to burn her alive if she would not join with them in their impious cries.
quotes.work: Dionysius of Alexandria, Letter to Fabius of Antioch, quoted in Eusebius, Church History VI.41.7
