hildegard-of-bingen.heroSummary: St. Hildegard of Bingen (1098–1179) was a Benedictine abbess on the Rhine who wrote visionary theology, composed sacred music, and challenged church leaders and an emperor by letter. Benedict XVI recognized her as a saint for the whole Church in May 2012 and named her a Doctor of the Church that October. Her optional memorial is September 17.
hildegard-of-bingen.searchDescription: St. Hildegard of Bingen (1098–1179), feast September 17: Benedictine abbess, visionary writer, composer of sacred music, and Doctor of the Church.

symbols.meaning: The opening miniature of the Rupertsberg Scivias shows fire pouring onto her head. It recalls her own account of a fiery light from the open heavens in 1141 that filled her mind and set her heart aflame, a call to write that the abbey describes as Pentecost-like.
In the same miniature she writes on wax tablets while the monk Volmar assists her, a reminder that her visions were written down with help and submitted to the Church's judgment.
Her three visionary works, Scivias, the Book of Life's Merits, and the Book of Divine Works, along with her letters and songs, which ground her title as Doctor of the Church.

symbols.symbol: Benedictine habit, often with an abbess's staff
symbols.meaning: Her life under the Rule of St. Benedict and her responsibility for the communities at Rupertsberg and Eibingen.

hildegard-of-bingen.whyWeTurn: People turn to Hildegard when they want faith and intelligence to stay together. She loved Scripture, music, and the created world, and she saw all of it coming from God and finding its center in Christ. She was also careful: she feared her visions might be illusions until wiser people had tested them, and she accepted the Church's judgment. Then she spoke plainly, even to an emperor, when she believed the Church was being harmed. Catholics ask her prayers for courage in telling the truth, for those who make sacred music, and for reverent care of creation. Her medieval notes on health belong to their time; her lasting gift is her teaching about God.

quotes.text: Praise him with sound of trumpet: praise him with psaltery and harp. Praise him with timbrel and choir: praise him with strings and organs. Praise him on high sounding cymbals: praise him on cymbals of joy: let every spirit praise the Lord. Alleluia.

prayer.text: Living God, you filled St. Hildegard with your light and gave her a voice to praise you in word and song. Through her prayers, open my eyes to your glory in Scripture, in the liturgy, and in the world you have made. Give me the humility to let others test what I think I have heard, and the courage to speak the truth with love when silence would be easier. Let my whole life become a song in harmony with your will, until I join the praise of heaven. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

link.label: Benedictine Abbey of St. Hildegard, Eibingen

feastCustoms: Attend Mass on September 17, her optional memorial in the General Roman Calendar since 2021; St. Robert Bellarmine shares the date, so a parish may honor either saint that day.
Listen to, or sing, one of her chants from the Symphonia, the collection of hymns and antiphons she composed for her sisters' worship.
In Germany, pilgrims gather at Eibingen, in Rüdesheim am Rhein, on September 17, when the shrine holding her relics is carried in procession through the village.
Read Benedict XVI's two 2010 catecheses on her, then read a short passage from Scivias with that guidance in mind.
Spend time outdoors thanking God for creation, remembering that her nature writings are medieval reflections and not medical advice.

hildegard-of-bingen.confirmationNote: Hildegard suits a Confirmation candidate who loves to learn, make music or art, or study the natural world, and who wants all of it to lead to God. She also shows that gifts need testing: she sought counsel and accepted the Church's judgment before speaking publicly. Choosing her means praying for both humility and courage, and being ready to speak the truth even when it costs something.
reflectionPrompts: Where have I sensed God's light in my life, and whom could I trust to help me test it honestly?
This week, listen to one of Hildegard's chants, or sing the hymns at Mass with full attention, and offer that music to God as praise.
Read Benedict XVI's general audiences on Hildegard of September 1 and 8, 2010, and note what he says about discernment and obedience.

ignatius-of-loyola.heroSummary: St. Ignatius of Loyola was a Basque nobleman whose wound at Pamplona in 1521 began a slow, searching conversion. He wrote the Spiritual Exercises, gathered the companions who became the Society of Jesus, and led the Jesuits from Rome until his death on July 31, 1556, the date of his feast.
ignatius-of-loyola.searchDescription: St. Ignatius of Loyola (1491–1556), feast July 31: the Basque soldier turned pilgrim who wrote the Spiritual Exercises and founded the Jesuits.

symbols.meaning: The Holy Name of Jesus, adopted as the emblem of the Society of Jesus.
"For the greater glory of God," the Jesuit motto; the book also recalls the Spiritual Exercises and the Society's Constitutions.
His vigil at Montserrat, where he laid down his sword before Our Lady and set aside his military ambitions.
His ordination and his service as a priest and first superior general of the Jesuits.

ignatius-of-loyola.whyWeTurn: People turn to Ignatius when they need to make a decision and want to know where God is in it. His own conversion was not tidy: a shattered leg, long boredom, books he had not chosen, a year of struggle at Manresa. Out of that he learned to notice which desires left lasting peace and which left him empty, and he wrote it down so others could pray the same way. Many Catholics ask his prayers before a retreat, a vocation choice, or a hard change of direction. He reminds us that God can be found in ordinary life, study, and work.

quotes.text: Man is created to praise, reverence, and serve God our Lord, and by this means to save his soul.
love ought to be put more in deeds than in words.
quotes.work: Spiritual Exercises, Contemplation to Gain Love, opening note

prayer.text: Take, Lord, and receive all my liberty, my memory, my intellect, and all my will--all that I have and possess. Thou gavest it to me: to Thee, Lord, I return it! All is Thine, dispose of it according to all Thy will. Give me Thy love and grace, for this is enough for me.
prayer.source: St. Ignatius of Loyola, Spiritual Exercises, Contemplation to Gain Love, translated by Elder Mullan, S.J. (1914)
prayer.note: Known as the Suscipe. Ignatius gives it in the Exercises as the retreatant's offering of self; many modern versions use different wording. This is Mullan's public-domain text exactly.

link.label: Read the Spiritual Exercises (Mullan translation) at CCEL

feastCustoms: July 31 is his memorial in the General Roman Calendar; join a parish for Mass, especially at a Jesuit church if one is nearby.
Begin a daily examination of conscience, a short prayer the Spiritual Exercises recommend for reviewing the day with God.
Pray the Suscipe slowly, offering God your freedom, memory, understanding, and will.
Plan a retreat based on the Spiritual Exercises; many Jesuit retreat houses and parishes offer guided retreats, including ones made in daily life.
Pray for the pope, since the first Jesuits offered themselves to him for whatever mission he chose.

ignatius-of-loyola.confirmationNote: Ignatius suits a Confirmation candidate who is still working out what to do with life. He did not begin holy; he began ambitious, then learned to pay attention to how God moved in his desires. Choosing him is a commitment to daily prayer, honest self-examination, and generous service, and to letting the Holy Spirit shape real decisions about study, work, and vocation.

Tonight, take five minutes to review the day: give thanks for one gift, notice one failure, and ask for help with tomorrow.

joachim.heroSummary: St. Joachim is honored by tradition as the father of the Virgin Mary, husband of St. Anne and grandfather of Jesus. Scripture never names him: his name and the story of his long wait for a child come from the second-century Protoevangelium of James. The Church celebrates Joachim and Anne together on July 26.

symbols.symbol: Lamb, or a lamb brought to the altar
symbols.meaning: The offering he brought to the Temple. In the Protoevangelium he is told he may not offer first because he has no child; later legend turns this into a priest refusing his gift.
Another image of his Temple offerings and of the prayer for a child that, in the tradition, God answered.
The Protoevangelium pictures him as a wealthy man with flocks who withdrew to the wilderness to fast and pray for forty days.
Later tradition places his joyful meeting with Anne here after angels announce Mary's birth; the Protoevangelium says only that Anne stood 'by the gate'.
His place as Mary's father, who in the tradition presents her to the priests for a blessing and later brings her to the Temple.

joachim.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Joachim as a father and grandfather, someone who waited, prayed and handed on faith. Scripture tells us nothing about him, not even his name; the story comes from an early noncanonical writing and long devotion. In that story he is shamed for having no child, goes into the wilderness to fast, and refuses to eat until God answers him. Tradition holds that the answer was Mary. Fathers, grandfathers, couples longing for children and anyone carrying a long, unanswered prayer find in him a steady companion. With Anne, he reminds the Church that grandparents are often where faith first takes root.

quotes.text: But these were men of mercy, whose godly deeds have not failed: Good things continue with their seed, Their posterity are a holy inheritance, and their seed hath stood in the covenants.
quotes.work: Ecclesiasticus (Sirach) 44:10–12, chosen for context; it is not about Joachim

quotes.text: And mayest thou see thy children's children, peace upon Israel.
quotes.work: Psalm 127:6 (Psalm 128:6 in modern numbering), chosen for context; it is not about Joachim

prayer.text: Lord God, the Church has long honored St. Joachim as the father of the Virgin Mary and the grandfather of your Son. Through his prayers, bless fathers and grandfathers, and all who wait a long time for an answer from you. Give them patience when you seem silent, humility when they feel overlooked, and joy in the gifts you send. Help us to honor the older people in our lives and to receive the faith they hand on, so that our families may be places where your promises are remembered. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

feastCustoms: Attend Mass on July 26, the memorial of Sts. Joachim and Anne, parents of the Blessed Virgin Mary; when it falls on a Sunday, the Sunday liturgy takes its place.
Honor your grandparents on the day, a long custom tied to this feast: visit, call or pray with them, or remember them at Mass if they have died.

Keep the World Day for Grandparents and the Elderly, which Pope Francis set on the fourth Sunday of July near this feast; some bishops' conferences, including in the United States, observe it on another Sunday.
Pray especially for fathers, grandfathers and couples longing for a child.
In the Byzantine tradition, Eastern Catholics honor Joachim and Anne on September 9, the day after the Nativity of Mary.
joachim.confirmationNote: Joachim suits a confirmand who is grateful for a father, grandfather or godparent who handed on the faith. Nothing he said or did is recorded in Scripture, so choosing him is a choice to honor patient, hidden faithfulness and prayer that keeps going when answers are slow. Confirmation strengthens Christians to witness to Christ, and much of that witness happens in families, from one generation to the next.
reflectionPrompts: What prayer have I been carrying for a long time, and can I offer it to God again today with trust?
Thank a father, grandfather or older mentor this week for something he taught you about faith.
Read the Catholic Encyclopedia article on St. Joachim and chapters 1–5 of the Protoevangelium of James, noting what the Encyclopedia treats as uncertain.

Husband of his daughter Mary and fellow member of Jesus' family
Mary's kinswoman, whose long-childless family also received a child as God's gift
A canonized father remembered for handing on faith to his daughters

joan-of-arc.heroSummary: St. Joan of Arc is honored by many Catholics as a patron of prisoners and captives, fitting for a young woman who spent her final year in custody. Raised at Domremy, she believed God called her to aid Charles VII. She was condemned and burned in 1431, cleared in 1456, and canonized in 1920.
joan-of-arc.searchDescription: St. Joan of Arc (1412–1431), feast May 30: the young Frenchwoman who answered God's call, was tried and burned at Rouen, and was canonized in 1920.

symbols.symbol: White banner with lilies and the names "Jhesus Maria"
symbols.meaning: At her trial Joan described her own standard: white cloth sprinkled with lilies, the world shown with an angel on each side, and the names of Jesus and Mary. She said she carried it into battle and valued it far above her sword.
Her documented place in the 1429 campaign that relieved Orléans and led to Charles VII's coronation at Reims; artists usually show her as a young woman in armor.
Her military role, though she testified that she had never killed anyone and carried her banner in attacks for that reason.
The French crown she served; she testified that the king granted her brothers arms bearing two golden lilies and a sword.
Her execution by burning at Rouen in May 1431, after a trial later annulled in 1456.

joan-of-arc.whyWeTurn: People turn to Joan when they feel small against forces far larger than themselves. She was a teenager with no rank or schooling, yet she trusted that God could use her. Her trial record lets us hear her own voice: frightened at times, but honest, quick, and unwilling to claim more about her soul than she knew. Because she spent her last year as a prisoner and was condemned by a court later found unjust, many Catholics ask her prayers for prisoners, captives, and anyone wrongly accused. Others look to her for courage to keep faith with their conscience under pressure.

quotes.text: If I am not, may God place me there; if I am, may God so keep me. I should be the saddest in all the world if I knew that I were not in the grace of God.
quotes.work: Trial of Condemnation, public examination of February 24, 1431 (answering whether she knew she was in God's grace)
quotes.translation: T. Douglas Murray, ed., Jeanne d'Arc, Maid of Orleans (1902), public domain

quotes.text: Better, forty times better, my banner than my sword!
quotes.work: Trial of Condemnation, public examination of February 27, 1431
quotes.translation: T. Douglas Murray, ed., Jeanne d'Arc, Maid of Orleans (1902), public domain

quotes.text: It was I, myself, who bore this banner, when I attacked the enemy, to save killing any one, for I have never killed any one.
quotes.work: Trial of Condemnation, public examination of February 27, 1431
quotes.translation: T. Douglas Murray, ed., Jeanne d'Arc, Maid of Orleans (1902), public domain

prayer.text: Saint Joan of Arc, you trusted God when you were young, unknown, and afraid, and you kept calling on the name of Jesus to the very end. Pray for all who are imprisoned, held captive, or wrongly accused, that they may find mercy, justice, and hope. Pray for me when I must speak the truth before people who misunderstand me. Help me to stay honest without bitterness, brave without pride, and humble enough to say only what I truly know. Ask the Lord to keep me in his grace, and if I have strayed from it, to bring me back. Amen.

feastCustoms: May 30, the anniversary of her death, is her commemoration in the Roman Martyrology rather than a memorial on the General Roman Calendar; ask her intercession at a weekday Mass or in personal prayer.
Pray slowly with the Holy Name of Jesus, the name Joan called on as she died, for example by praying the Litany of the Holy Name.
Pray for prisoners, captives, and people awaiting trial, and consider supporting a parish or diocesan prison ministry.
In Orléans, the cathedral celebrates a solemn Mass in her honor each May 8 during the city's festivities marking its liberation in 1429.
Read a few of her answers from the trial record and notice how she spoke about God, conscience, and grace.

places.name: Cathedral of Sainte-Croix, Orléans

joan-of-arc.confirmationNote: Joan can be a strong Confirmation saint for someone who feels young or overlooked but wants to act on faith. She asks the confirmed to listen for God's call, to pray steadily, and to tell the truth even when it costs something. Choosing her also means learning her real history, including her trial and the Church's later reversal of its verdict, rather than only the heroic legend.
reflectionPrompts: Joan refused to claim certainty she did not have about her own soul. Where am I tempted to overstate or hide the truth about myself before God?
Write a short note, offer a prayer, or give practical support this week to someone who is in prison or feels trapped by circumstances.
Read her answers from the February 24, 1431 examination in T. Douglas Murray's 1902 translation of the trial record and note how she responds to trick questions.

john-berchmans.heroSummary: St. John Berchmans was a Flemish Jesuit student who died in Rome in 1621, aged twenty-two, before he could be ordained. Fellow Jesuits remembered the care he gave to prayer, study, and the ordinary duties of community life. Jesuits celebrate him on November 26, and many altar servers and students look to him as a model.
john-berchmans.searchDescription: St. John Berchmans, Jesuit student who died at 22 in 1621, remembered for doing ordinary duties with great care. Symbols, prayer and November 26 feast.

symbols.meaning: His love for Christ crucified; as he was dying he asked for his crucifix, and his statues show him holding it.
His faithful keeping of the rule of the Society of Jesus, which the Catholic Encyclopedia singles out as the mark of his holiness.
His devotion to Mary; the rosary was among the three things he asked to hold at the end, and it appears in his statues.

john-berchmans.whyWeTurn: People turn to John Berchmans because his holiness was ordinary in the best sense. He never preached a famous sermon or traveled as a missionary. He studied hard, kept the rule of his community, prayed the rosary, and stayed kind to those around him, even after losing both parents during his years of formation. The Catholic Encyclopedia describes him as a saint who did ordinary actions with extraordinary perfection. That makes him a natural companion for students, altar servers, and anyone tempted to think small duties do not matter. Asking his prayers is a way of asking for faithfulness in whatever is in front of you today.

quotes.text: If I do not become a saint when I am young, I shall never become one.
quotes.work: Saying recorded in the Catholic Encyclopedia, "St. John Berchmans" (1910)
quotes.translation: Catholic Encyclopedia English text (1910, public domain)

quotes.text: My penance is to live the common life.
quotes.work: Saying recorded in the Catholic Encyclopedia, "St. John Berchmans" (1910)
quotes.translation: Catholic Encyclopedia English text (1910, public domain)

quotes.text: He that is faithful in that which is least, is faithful also in that which is greater.

prayer.text: Lord Jesus, you made Saint John Berchmans holy in the middle of classes, chores, and community life. Through his prayers, help me do the small things in front of me with care and love: my studies, my work, my promises, and my prayers. When no one notices, remind me that you do. Keep me close to you on the cross and close to your Mother in the rosary, and make me faithful to the commitments I have made. Give young people the courage to want holiness now, not someday. Amen.

feastCustoms: Jesuit communities and schools keep his feast on November 26; the Roman Martyrology also remembers him on August 13, the day he died in 1621.
Pray for and thank the altar servers in your parish; Catholic Culture lists him as a patron of altar servers and young people.
Pray a decade of the rosary, one of the devotions he held on to as he was dying.
Pick one ordinary duty, such as homework, a chore, or arriving on time, and do it as carefully as you can as an offering to God.
In Rome, visit the Jesuit Church of Sant'Ignazio, where his body rests.

places.name: Church of Sant'Ignazio di Loyola

john-berchmans.confirmationNote: John Berchmans suits a Confirmation candidate who is still in school and wonders whether holiness has to wait. He was a student who prayed, studied, and kept his commitments with steady care, and he died young without doing anything the world would call remarkable. Choosing his name can be a commitment to faithfulness in small duties, love for the Eucharist and Mary, and wanting to be a saint now.
reflectionPrompts: Which ordinary duty in your week do you treat as unimportant, and how might you offer it to God instead?
Choose one small commitment, such as being on time or finishing an assignment carefully, and keep it faithfully for seven days.
Read Luke 16:10 and 1 Timothy 4:12 in the Douay-Rheims, then read the Catholic Encyclopedia article on St. John Berchmans and note what his fellow Jesuits remembered about him.

john-the-baptist.heroSummary: St. John the Baptist is the prophet who prepared the way for Jesus, calling people to repentance and baptizing in the Jordan. The Church celebrates his birth with a solemnity on June 24 and his martyrdom under Herod Antipas on August 29. His whole mission pointed beyond himself: "He must increase, but I must decrease."
john-the-baptist.searchDescription: St. John the Baptist, feasts June 24 (his birth) and August 29 (his martyrdom): the prophet who baptized Jesus and pointed others to Christ.

symbols.meaning: Recalls his words on seeing Jesus, "Behold the Lamb of God" (John 1:29): John's task was to point others to Christ.

symbols.symbol: Cross-tipped staff, often with a banner
symbols.meaning: Announces the victory of Christ, whose coming and saving death John proclaimed.
The rough clothing Matthew 3:4 describes, the dress of a desert prophet who lived simply and called others to penance.
His martyrdom: Herod had him beheaded and the head brought on a dish to Herodias' daughter (Matthew 14:8–11).
Marks him as a prophet; Vatican News calls him the last of Israel's great prophets and the first to bear witness to Jesus.

john-the-baptist.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. John the Baptist when they need courage to tell the truth and humility to step aside. He drew large crowds, yet he pointed his own disciples toward Jesus and said his joy was complete when Christ became greater. He asked people to change their lives in concrete ways, and he paid with his life for telling a powerful ruler that his marriage was wrong. Catholics remember him at every baptism, since he baptized Jesus in the Jordan. He is a natural companion for parents, godparents, catechists and anyone whose work is to prepare the way for others and then let Christ take the center.

quotes.text: Do penance: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.
Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who taketh away the sin of the world.
He must increase, but I must decrease.

prayer.text: St. John the Baptist, you prepared the way of the Lord and pointed others to the Lamb of God. Pray for me, that I may turn away from whatever keeps me from Christ and make straight the paths of my life. Give me courage to speak the truth with love, even when it costs me, and the humility to rejoice when others draw closer to Jesus than to me. Help me to remember my baptism and to live it each day. May Christ increase in me, and may I decrease. Amen.

feastCustoms: Attend Mass on June 24, the Solemnity of the Nativity of St. John the Baptist, the highest rank of feast; its date follows Luke 1:36, six months before Christmas.
Keep August 29, the memorial of his Passion, by reading the Gospel account of his death (Mark 6:17–29) and praying for those who suffer for telling the truth.

In many places, especially in Europe and Brazil, communities light St. John's fires on the eve of the feast, recalling John as "a burning and a shining light" (John 5:35); a family can light a candle or bless a small fire at home.
Sing or read the hymn Ut queant laxis, written for his feast, whose opening syllables gave names to the notes of the musical scale.
Find out the date of your baptism, renew your baptismal promises, and thank God for the people who brought you to the font.

places.name: Archbasilica of St. John Lateran

john-the-baptist.confirmationNote: John the Baptist suits a confirmand who wants courage to speak truthfully and the humility to let Christ come first. He prepared others to meet Jesus, baptized him in the Jordan, and accepted prison and death rather than flatter a king. Confirmation strengthens Christians to witness to Christ in word and deed, and John's own words, "He must increase, but I must decrease," make a fitting promise for that new strength.
reflectionPrompts: Where in my life do I need Christ to increase and my own need for attention to decrease?
This week, point someone toward a good you did not create: credit a colleague's work, encourage a friend's faith, or invite someone to Mass.
Read Luke 1:57–80 and John 3:22–30 in the Douay-Rheims, and compare what Zachary prophesied about his son with what John later says about himself.

joseph.heroSummary: St. Joseph is patron of the universal Church and of workers, and Catholic sources also name him a patron of immigrants and of children. The Gospels present him as Mary's husband and the righteous man who protected Jesus. The Church honors him on March 19 and as Joseph the Worker on May 1.
joseph.searchDescription: St. Joseph, Mary's husband and guardian of Jesus, is patron of the universal Church and workers. Feast: March 19, with Joseph the Worker on May 1.

symbols.symbol: The Child Jesus in his arms
symbols.meaning: His role as the guardian and earthly father who cared for Jesus.
His trade (Matthew 13:55) and the dignity of ordinary work, honored on May 1.
A traditional sign of purity, reflecting his chaste love for Mary.

joseph.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Joseph because he was trusted with the most ordinary and most important things: a family, a home, a day's work. The Gospels never record a word from him, yet they show him acting, taking Mary into his home, fleeing to Egypt, settling in Nazareth. Parents, workers, migrants and anyone carrying responsibility quietly find a friend in him. The Church has named him patron of the universal Church, and many Catholics also ask his prayers as they prepare for a happy death. Asking Joseph's help is a way of learning to listen to God, then act faithfully.

quotes.text: Joseph, son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife, for that which is conceived in her, is of the Holy Ghost.
And Joseph rising up from sleep, did as the angel of the Lord had commanded him, and took unto him his wife.

prayer.text: To thee, O blessed Joseph, we have recourse in our affliction, and having implored the help of thy thrice holy Spouse, we now, with hearts filled with confidence, earnestly beg thee also to take us under thy protection. By that charity wherewith thou wert united to the Immaculate Virgin Mother of God, and by that fatherly love with which thou didst cherish the Child Jesus, we beseech thee and we humbly pray that thou wilt look down with gracious eye upon that inheritance which Jesus Christ purchased by His blood, and wilt succor us in our need by thy power and strength. Defend, O most watchful guardian of the Holy Family, the chosen off-spring of Jesus Christ. Keep from us, O most loving Father, all blight of error and corruption. Aid us from on high, most valiant defender, in this conflict with the powers of darkness. And even as of old thou didst rescue the Child Jesus from the peril of His life, so now defend God's Holy Church from the snares of the enemy and from all adversity. Shield us ever under thy patronage, that, following thine example and strengthened by thy help, we may live a holy life, die a happy death, and attain to everlasting bliss in Heaven. Amen.
prayer.source: Pope Leo XIII, encyclical Quamquam Pluries (1889), English text on vatican.va
prayer.note: Leo XIII asked that this prayer be added to the Rosary during October.

link.label: Quamquam Pluries on vatican.va

Keep March, traditionally dedicated to St. Joseph, and Wednesdays through the year as days for a prayer to him.
In Sicily and many Italian-American parishes, families prepare a St. Joseph's Table of breads, sweets and flowers, have it blessed and share the food with guests.
In October, add Leo XIII's prayer to St. Joseph at the end of the Rosary, as he requested.
On May 1, pray for workers and for anyone looking for a job.

joseph.confirmationNote: Joseph suits a confirmand who wants to grow in quiet faithfulness. Scripture records none of his words, only what he did when God asked something hard of him: he listened, rose and acted. Confirmation strengthens a Christian to live the faith in daily life, and Joseph shows what that looks like in work, in family and in protecting others who depend on us.
reflectionPrompts: Whom has God entrusted to your care, and how can you protect them this week?
Do one piece of ordinary work today carefully and offer it to God, as Joseph did at Nazareth.
Read Matthew 1:18–25 and 2:13–23 and notice how often Joseph acts without speaking.

jude-thaddeus.heroSummary: St. Jude Thaddeus is one of the Twelve Apostles, invoked as the patron of desperate situations and listed as a patron of hospitals. Catholics celebrate him with St. Simon on October 28. He is not Judas Iscariot, and devotion to him grew as the saint people turn to when every other door seems closed.

symbols.symbol: Medallion with the face of Christ
symbols.meaning: Recalls the tradition of the Image of Edessa, a legend in which Jude carries a cloth bearing Christ's face to the ailing King Abgar.
The Holy Spirit descending on the apostles at Pentecost.
Traditional accounts of his martyrdom, which differ and cannot be confirmed historically.
Hope and renewal, like new growth in spring, fitting his role as a saint of hope in hard times.
The Letter of Jude in the New Testament, which tradition attributes to him.

jude-thaddeus.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Jude when a situation feels beyond repair: a diagnosis, a broken relationship, a debt, a prayer that seems to go unanswered. Tradition holds that his name, so close to that of Judas Iscariot, kept many Christians from calling on him for centuries, so he became the apostle people approached when they had tried everything else. Devotion grew from that start into one of the most popular in the Church, especially through shrines in the Americas. Asking Jude's help is not a formula for a guaranteed outcome. It is a way of refusing to give up on God, bringing the hardest things into prayer with a friend of Christ who knows what it means to be overlooked.

quotes.text: But you, my beloved, building yourselves upon your most holy faith, praying in the Holy Ghost, keep yourselves in the love of God, waiting for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ, unto life everlasting.

Now to him who is able to preserve you without sin, and to present you spotless before the presence of his glory with exceeding joy, in the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, to the only God our Saviour through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory and magnificence, empire and power, before all ages, and now, and for all ages of ages. Amen.

prayer.text: St. Jude, apostle and friend of Jesus, you know what it is to be misunderstood and overlooked. I bring you the need I have almost stopped praying about. Ask the Lord to give me patience while I wait, courage to do what is mine to do, and peace when the answer is not the one I wanted. Keep me building on the faith I received, praying in the Holy Spirit, and trusting in the mercy of Christ. Help me to hope again. Amen.

Bring to prayer one intention you had quietly given up on, and pray Jude 1:20–21 over it.
Wear or display green, the color linked with St. Jude as a sign of hope.

He is an apostle, so the name ties you to the foundation of the Church, and the short Letter of Jude, which tradition attributes to him, urges believers to build on their faith, pray in the Holy Spirit and keep themselves in God's love. Choosing him is a quiet promise not to give up on prayer.

Write down one intention you had given up on and pray for it each day for nine days.
Read the Letter of Jude (one chapter) and note what verses 20–21 ask believers to do.

lioba.heroSummary: St. Lioba, also called Leoba, was an English nun who answered the call of her relative St. Boniface and became the first abbess of Tauberbischofsheim in the Frankish lands. Remembered as a learned teacher and wise leader of women, she died around 782. The Diocese of Mainz keeps her memorial on September 28.
lioba.searchDescription: St. Lioba (Leoba), English nun called by her relative St. Boniface to lead the abbey of Tauberbischofsheim: teacher, abbess and letter-writer. Feast: Sept. 28.
lioba.whyWeTurn: People turn to Lioba because she shows what steady, learned faith can build. She left England to support a mission in unfamiliar lands, and she did it by teaching, governing a community, and forming women in prayer and Scripture. Her surviving letter to Boniface is humble and warm: she asks him to pray for her late father and her ailing mother, admits she is still practicing her verse, and asks him to correct her writing. Students, teachers, and women in leadership can find in her a companion who joined learning with humility. To ask her prayers is to ask for wisdom, perseverance far from home, and friendships that lead to God.

quotes.text: And this I beg of thee fervently, beloved brother, to guard me with the shield of thy prayers, against the poisoned shafts of the hidden enemy.
quotes.work: Letter of Lioba to Boniface (Kylie no. XXIII)
quotes.translation: Edward Kylie, The English Correspondence of Saint Boniface (1911, public domain)

quotes.text: The art I have learned from the teaching of Eadburga, who continues without ceasing to search into the divine law.
quotes.work: Letter of Lioba to Boniface (Kylie no. XXIII)
quotes.translation: Edward Kylie, The English Correspondence of Saint Boniface (1911, public domain)

prayer.text: God of wisdom, you called Saint Lioba from her home in England to teach and guide a community in a new land. Through her prayers, give me a love for your word and the patience to keep learning. Bless all who teach, all who lead communities of faith, and all who live far from home. Help me to ask for prayers humbly and to give them faithfully, especially for the members of my family who have died. Guard me with the shield of your grace, and keep me rooted in prayer and steady in service. Amen.
prayer.note: The phrase 'shield of your grace' echoes her letter to Boniface, in which she asks him to guard her with the shield of his prayers.

feastCustoms: In the Diocese of Mainz, September 28 is an optional memorial of St. Lioba, abbess of Tauberbischofsheim; elsewhere, remember her in personal or family prayer that day.
Pray for missionaries and for women who lead religious communities, two of the intentions the Diocese of Mainz suggests for her day.
Pray for a parent or relative who has died, as Lioba asked Boniface to pray for her father.
Write to a mentor, teacher, or godparent to thank them and ask for their prayers, following the example of her letter to Boniface.
Spend time with Scripture or a solid book about the faith to honor her as a teacher; near Fulda, her relics are venerated in the church on the Petersberg.
lioba.confirmationNote: Lioba suits a Confirmation candidate who loves learning or feels drawn to teach and lead. She left home to help build the Church in a new land, not through dramatic deeds but through study, prayer, and the patient formation of a community. Her letter to Boniface shows humility and a habit of asking for prayer. Choosing her name can be a commitment to growing in knowledge of the faith and sharing it with others.
reflectionPrompts: Who taught you the faith, and how might you thank them this week?
Write a short note to a mentor or relative asking for their prayers, and promise to pray for them in return.
Read Lioba's letter to Boniface (no. XXIII) in Edward Kylie's The English Correspondence of Saint Boniface (1911) and notice what she asks for and why.

maria-mazzarello.heroSummary: St. Maria Domenica Mazzarello was a farmer's daughter from Mornese, Italy, who, after typhoid ended her work in the fields, began teaching village girls to sew, pray, and love God. With St. John Bosco she cofounded the Daughters of Mary Help of Christians in 1872. Salesians keep her feast on May 13.
maria-mazzarello.searchDescription: St. Maria Domenica Mazzarello, farm girl from Mornese who cofounded the Salesian Sisters with John Bosco in 1872. Feast: May 13.

symbols.symbol: Habit of the Daughters of Mary Help of Christians
symbols.meaning: Her religious profession in 1872 and her role as first superior of the Salesian Sisters.
The dressmaking workshop she opened in Mornese after her illness, where girls learned a trade along with prayer and the love of God.
The young people at the heart of her mission: the workshop, the festive oratory, and a home for girls without families.

symbols.symbol: Image of Mary Help of Christians
symbols.meaning: The title of Mary that gives her congregation its name; her body rests in the Basilica of Mary Help of Christians in Turin.

maria-mazzarello.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Maria Mazzarello because her holiness grew out of an ordinary, limited life. She was a strong farm girl until typhoid, caught while nursing sick relatives, took that strength away. Instead of giving up, she learned dressmaking and opened a small workshop where village girls learned a trade, prayed, and found friendship. Her Salesian sisters remember her cheerfulness and her habit of teaching that work, study, and play could all be offered to God. Parents, teachers, and anyone who works with young people ask her help to guide them with warmth and good sense. She is also a friend to those whose plans were changed by illness.

quotes.text: Rejoice in the Lord always; again, I say, rejoice.
Whatsoever you do, do it from the heart, as to the Lord, and not to men: Knowing that you shall receive of the Lord the reward of inheritance. Serve ye the Lord Christ.

prayer.text: Lord God, you led Saint Maria Domenica Mazzarello through illness to a new way of serving you, teaching girls to work, to pray, and to love you. Through her prayers, help me accept the limits I did not choose and find in them a door to serve others. Make my ordinary work an offering to you, done with care and a cheerful heart. Bless all young people, especially girls who lack opportunity or a home, and bless those who teach and guide them. Mary, Help of Christians, pray for us. Amen.

feastCustoms: Join a Salesian school, parish, or community for her feast on May 13; it belongs to the Salesian family's calendar rather than the universal Roman calendar, and she died on May 14, 1881.
Teach someone a practical skill you have, such as sewing, cooking, or a repair, as she did in her Mornese workshop.
Offer your ordinary work, study, or play to God at the start of the day, in the spirit she taught her sisters.

Make a short visit to a church to pray before the Blessed Sacrament; Salesian accounts remember the small window at the Valponasca farmhouse that became her place of prayer because it faced the church.
Pray for, or support, the Salesian Sisters' schools and missions, which began reaching South America in 1877 during her lifetime.

places.name: Basilica of Mary Help of Christians (resting place of her remains)

maria-mazzarello.confirmationNote: St. Maria Mazzarello can suit a Confirmation candidate who expects to work with young people or who has had to rethink plans after illness or setback. She turned a physical limitation into a new mission, teaching practical skills alongside faith. She was remembered for cheerfulness and good sense as a leader. Choosing her name can mean committing to steady, joyful service in ordinary places.
reflectionPrompts: Is there a limitation in your life that you have only seen as a loss? Ask how God might use it to open another way of serving.
Pick one skill you know well and offer to teach it to a younger person or a friend this month.
Read Colossians 3:12–24, then read the Salesian Missions biography of Mary Mazzarello and note how she joined practical work with prayer.

maximilian-kolbe.heroSummary: St. Maximilian Maria Kolbe is a patron of prisoners, honored for the life he gave at Auschwitz in place of a condemned man. A Polish Conventual Franciscan, he founded a Marian movement, built a publishing apostolate at Niepokalanów, and served as a missionary in Japan. Catholics keep his memorial on August 14.
maximilian-kolbe.searchDescription: St. Maximilian Kolbe, Polish Franciscan, Marian publisher and missionary, who gave his life for another prisoner at Auschwitz in 1941. Feast: August 14.

symbols.symbol: Two crowns, one white and one red
symbols.meaning: Purity and martyrdom, from a childhood vision of Mary that he described to his mother; known through her recollection.

symbols.symbol: Striped prisoner's uniform with the number 16670
symbols.meaning: His imprisonment at Auschwitz from May 1941 and his death there for another prisoner.
His life as a Conventual Franciscan friar and priest.
The outward sign of consecration to Mary he gave the Militia of the Immaculata.
The Knight of the Immaculata and his publishing work at Niepokalanów.

maximilian-kolbe.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Maximilian Kolbe because his final act was so concrete. In Auschwitz, when ten men were condemned to starve in reprisal for an escape, he stepped forward to take the place of Franciszek Gajowniczek, a husband and father who survived the war. Prisoners, families, and anyone facing cruelty find in him a friend who knew captivity from the inside. His death did not come out of nowhere: for years he had given himself to Mary and to spreading the faith through presses, magazines, and missions. Many ask his help to love when love costs something, and to hope in places that seem built to destroy hope.

quotes.text: Greater love than this no man hath, that a man lay down his life for his friends.
And Mary said: Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word.

prayer.text: Lord Jesus, you gave Saint Maximilian a burning love for your Mother and the courage to lay down his life for another prisoner. Through his prayers, strengthen all who are imprisoned, unjustly held, or afraid. Comfort families torn apart by violence. Teach me to give myself to Mary as he did, to use my gifts and the tools of my time to make you known, and to answer hatred with love. When the hour of sacrifice comes, small or great, let me step forward and not hold back. Amen.

Pray the rosary or offer a Mass for prisoners and for people who suffer from human cruelty, as Catholic Culture suggests for his day.
Make or renew an act of consecration to Mary, the heart of the Militia of the Immaculata he founded in 1917.
Wear a Miraculous Medal, which he made the outward sign of that consecration.
Read about Auschwitz and the man he saved, Franciszek Gajowniczek, using the Auschwitz-Birkenau State Museum's account.

maximilian-kolbe.confirmationNote: St. Maximilian Kolbe can suit a Confirmation candidate who is drawn to courage, Mary, or communication. He used presses, magazines, and radio to share the faith, and he gave his life for a stranger at Auschwitz. Taking his name can mean committing to love that costs something, to standing with people who are imprisoned or forgotten, and to using today's media for good.
reflectionPrompts: Who in your life might need you to 'step forward' for them this week, even in a small and costly way?
Write a letter or card to someone in prison, or learn about a prison ministry in your parish or diocese.
Read John 15:12–17, then read the Auschwitz-Birkenau State Museum's account of his sacrifice and note how the Gospel and the history illuminate each other.

maximinus-of-aix.heroSummary: St. Maximin of Aix is honored as the patron of the diocese of Aix and is credited with the beginnings of Christian faith in Aix-en-Provence. His local feast is June 8. Provençal legend makes him one of Christ's seventy-two disciples who sailed to Provence with Mary Magdalene, Martha and Lazarus, but that voyage is tradition, not established history.
maximinus-of-aix.searchDescription: St. Maximin of Aix, feast June 8: patron of the diocese of Aix, credited with the city's first Christian preaching; the Bethany voyage is legend.
maximinus-of-aix.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Maximin to give thanks for those who first brought the faith to a place. Very little about his life can be documented: the Roman Martyrology simply credits him with the beginnings of Christian faith in Aix. Tradition holds much more, that he was one of the seventy-two disciples Jesus sent out and that he came to Provence with Mary Magdalene and the family of Bethany. Whatever the details, Catholics in Provence have kept his name in prayer for centuries. He is a fitting companion for anyone praying for their own diocese, for missionaries, and for people who share the faith quietly where it is new.

quotes.text: And after these things the Lord appointed also other seventy-two: and he sent them two and two before his face into every city and place whither he himself was to come.
The harvest indeed is great, but the labourers are few. Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he send labourers into his harvest.

prayer.text: Lord Jesus, you sent your disciples ahead of you into every town to prepare your way. We thank you for St. Maximin and for all who first carried the Gospel to Provence, and for those who first brought the faith to us. Bless our bishops and our parishes, and send labourers into your harvest. Whatever we know or do not know of our beginnings, keep us faithful to what we have received, and make us ready to hand it on with joy. Amen.

feastCustoms: June 8 is his feast in the diocese of Aix; elsewhere, remember him in personal prayer, since he is not on the General Roman Calendar. Do not confuse him with St. Maximin of Trier, honored on May 29.
Pray for your own bishop and diocese, and find out who first brought the faith to your area.
Read Luke 10:1–20, the sending of the seventy-two, and pray for missionaries and new Christian communities.

Pilgrims in Provence visit the basilica at Saint-Maximin-la-Sainte-Baume, where tradition places his tomb in the crypt, and Saint-Sauveur Cathedral in Aix, whose Romanesque nave local tradition links to an oratory he founded.
maximinus-of-aix.confirmationNote: Maximin could suit a confirmand who wants to honor the people who first handed on the faith, whether in a family or a region. Little about his life is certain beyond his long association with Aix, and the stories of his voyage with Mary Magdalene are legend. What remains is a simple witness: someone remembered for helping the Gospel take root where it was new. Confirmation sends every Christian to do the same where they live.
reflectionPrompts: Who first passed the faith on to me, and have I thanked God, and them, for it?
Find out who founded your parish or diocese, and pray for your current bishop by name this week.
Read Luke 10:1–20 and the Catholic Encyclopedia article 'Aix', and compare what history records about the first bishops of Aix with the Provençal tradition.

michael-the-archangel.heroSummary: St. Michael the Archangel is a patron of Brussels, whose cathedral is dedicated to him and St. Gudula, and he is invoked across the Church as a protector against evil. Scripture names him in Daniel, Jude and Revelation. Catholics honor him with Gabriel and Raphael on September 29.
michael-the-archangel.searchDescription: St. Michael the Archangel, honored September 29 with Gabriel and Raphael, appears in Daniel, Jude and Revelation as a heavenly protector against evil.

symbols.meaning: His role as leader of the heavenly host in the struggle against evil, drawn from Revelation 12.

symbols.symbol: Dragon or devil beneath his feet
symbols.meaning: The defeat of the dragon, 'that old serpent, who is called the devil and Satan', in Revelation 12.
A later tradition that pictures Michael weighing souls at judgment; this image does not come from Scripture.
He is an angel, a spiritual messenger of God rather than a human saint.
Leadership of God's angels; his name means 'Who is like God?'

michael-the-archangel.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Michael when they feel under attack, whether by temptation, fear, or forces they cannot name. His very name is a question, "Who is like God?", and it answers itself: no one is, and evil does not have the last word. Scripture shows him standing guard over God's people, not as a rival power but as a servant acting under God's authority. Soldiers, police officers and the sick have long asked his protection, and Pope Leo XIII wrote a prayer to him that many Catholics still say daily. Calling on Michael is a way of asking for courage and clear sight, and of remembering that the fight against evil is God's before it is ours.

quotes.text: And there was a great battle in heaven, Michael and his angels fought with the dragon, and the dragon fought and his angels: and they prevailed not, neither was their place found any more in heaven.
But at that time shall Michael rise up, the great prince, who standeth for the children of thy people.
When Michael the archangel, disputing with the devil, contended about the body of Moses, he durst not bring against him the judgment of railing speech, but said: The Lord command thee.

prayer.text: St. Michael the Archangel, defend us in battle, be our protection against the wickedness and snares of the Devil. May God rebuke him, we humbly pray. And do thou, O Prince of the Heavenly Host, by the Power of God, thrust into hell Satan and all evil spirits who wander the earth seeking the ruin of souls. Amen.
prayer.source: United States Catholic Catechism for Adults (USCCB), Prayer to St. Michael the Archangel
prayer.note: Composed by Pope Leo XIII in the 1880s and once recited after Low Mass; in 1994 St. John Paul II asked Catholics not to forget it. English wordings vary slightly; this is the USCCB text. The story of a vision behind the prayer is reported, not documented.

feastCustoms: Attend Mass on September 29, the feast of Sts. Michael, Gabriel and Raphael, Archangels, in the Roman calendar.
Pray the Prayer to St. Michael on the feast and make it a daily habit, as St. John Paul II encouraged.
In England and other countries the day is called Michaelmas; a traditional British meal is roast goose.
Decorate the home or table with Michaelmas daisies (purple asters), which bloom around the feast.
Read Revelation 12 or Daniel 10–12 as a family and talk about where you need courage against evil.

places.name: Cathedral of St. Michael and St. Gudula
Abbey of Mont-Saint-Michel (Monastic Fraternities of Jerusalem)

michael-the-archangel.confirmationNote: Michael is a fitting patron for a confirmand who wants courage. Confirmation strengthens a Christian to bear witness and resist evil, and Michael's name, "Who is like God?", keeps the focus on God rather than on our own strength. Because he is an archangel rather than a human saint, choosing him means asking a heavenly protector, not a role model with a life story, to stand with you.
reflectionPrompts: Where in your life do you most need courage to choose good over evil right now?
Pray the Prayer to St. Michael each morning this week, perhaps before leaving home.
Read Revelation 12:7–12 and Daniel 12:1–3 and note what each passage says Michael does.

monica.heroSummary: St. Monica (about 331–387) is honored as a patron of mothers. Born at Thagaste in North Africa, she was the wife of Patricius and the mother of St. Augustine of Hippo, for whose conversion she prayed for years. She saw him baptized in Milan and died at Ostia in 387. Her memorial is August 27.
monica.searchDescription: St. Monica (about 331–387), feast August 27: mother of St. Augustine, whose long prayers for her son are remembered in his Confessions.

symbols.meaning: Her years of weeping and prayer for Augustine. In the Confessions he recalls a bishop telling her that the son of these tears could not perish.
An Augustinian tradition, not history, says Mary appeared to the grieving Monica and gave her a leather belt to wear; the cincture later became the emblem of the Augustinian habit.
Her widowhood: she lost her husband Patricius when she was about 39 and went on managing the family's affairs.
Her love of Scripture and prayer, and the Confessions, the book in which Augustine preserved her words and their conversation at Ostia.

monica.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Monica when someone they love has drifted from God and nothing they say seems to help. Augustine remembers her weeping and praying for him for years, following him from Africa to Italy, and refusing to give up. He also remembers her patience in a hard marriage and her advice to other wives. Parents, spouses and grandparents ask her prayers for children and relatives far from the faith. Widows find in her someone who carried on after loss. Her last request, that her sons remember her at the Lord's altar, also makes her a gentle companion for those who pray for the dead.

quotes.text: One thing there was for which I desired to linger for a while in this life, that I might see thee a Catholic Christian before I died.
quotes.work: Augustine, Confessions, Book IX, chapter 10 (Monica's words to Augustine at Ostia)

quotes.text: Lay this body any where; let not the care for that any way disquiet you: this only I request, that you would remember me at the Lord's altar, wherever you be.
quotes.work: Augustine, Confessions, Book IX, chapter 11 (Monica's words to her sons before her death)

quotes.text: Go thy ways and God bless thee, for it is not possible that the son of these tears should perish.
quotes.work: Augustine, Confessions, Book III, chapter 12 (a bishop's answer to Monica's pleading)

prayer.text: Lord God, you heard the tears of St. Monica and, in your own time, brought her son Augustine home to you. Through her prayers, give me a patient and hopeful heart for the people I love who are far from you. Keep me from nagging, bitterness and despair, and teach me to pray, to wait and to love without giving up. Comfort all mothers, wives and widows who carry heavy hearts. And when my own life ends, let those I love remember me at your altar, as Monica asked. Amen.

link.label: Read Confessions Book IX (Monica at Ostia) at New Advent

feastCustoms: Attend Mass on August 27, her memorial in the General Roman Calendar, the day before the feast of her son St. Augustine on August 28.
Pray a novena to St. Monica in the nine days before her feast for a family member who has stopped practicing the faith.
Read Book IX, chapters 10–11 of the Confessions, Augustine's account of their conversation at Ostia and her death.
Arrange to have a Mass offered for a mother or grandmother who has died, honoring Monica's request to be remembered at the Lord's altar.
Write a note of thanks to a mother, grandmother or godmother whose prayers have carried you.
monica.confirmationNote: Monica suits a confirmand who wants to grow in faithful, persevering prayer, especially for family members. She was a laywoman, wife and mother whose faith was tested by a difficult marriage and a son who resisted God for years. Choosing her means committing to pray for others patiently and to trust that God works on his own timetable, even when change seems slow.
reflectionPrompts: Who in my life am I tempted to give up on, and how could I bring that person to God in prayer this week?
Choose one person who is far from God, write their name down, and pray for them by name every day for nine days.
Read Confessions Book IX, chapters 10–11, in Pusey's translation and notice how Augustine describes his mother at the end of her life.

relatedSaints.reason: Her son, whose conversion she prayed for and who recorded her life in the Confessions
Bishop of Milan who baptized Augustine while Monica was living there
Another wife and mother remembered for patience in a difficult marriage
Also invoked as a patron of mothers

mother-teresa.heroSummary: St. Teresa of Calcutta, known worldwide as Mother Teresa, was a Loreto sister and teacher who in 1946 felt a "call within a call" to serve the poorest people of Calcutta. She founded the Missionaries of Charity, whose homes for the sick, dying, and abandoned spread across the world. Catholics remember her on September 5.
mother-teresa.searchDescription: St. Teresa of Calcutta (Mother Teresa), founder of the Missionaries of Charity who served the sick and dying poor. Feast: September 5.

symbols.symbol: White cotton sari with blue borders
symbols.meaning: The simple habit she first put on in August 1948 when she left Loreto to serve the poor; her sisters still wear it.
The Holy See's biography describes her beginning each day with Jesus in the Eucharist and then going out to the slums with a rosary in her hand.
Christ's words from the Cross (John 19:28), written on the walls of Missionaries of Charity chapels as a reminder of Jesus' thirst for love and for souls.

symbols.symbol: A sick or dying person in her care
symbols.meaning: Her work for people left to die without care, which Pope Francis singled out in his canonization homily.

mother-teresa.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Teresa of Calcutta because she treated the people others overlooked as persons worth loving: the sick, the dying, and the abandoned. She saw in them Christ himself, taking literally the Gospel's words about the least of these. Her life was also simple and repeatable. She began each day with the Eucharist, carried a rosary, and did ordinary acts of care. Letters published after her death revealed years of spiritual darkness, a felt absence of God, and that makes her a quiet companion for anyone who keeps faith when prayer feels empty. Asking her prayers usually leads to something practical: noticing the lonely person nearby and doing something kind.

quotes.text: Afterwards, Jesus knowing that all things were now accomplished, that the scripture might be fulfilled, said: I thirst.
Amen I say to you, as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me.

prayer.text: Lord Jesus, from the Cross you said, "I thirst," and Saint Teresa of Calcutta heard in those words your longing for love and for souls. Through her prayers, open my eyes to the people around me who are hungry, sick, lonely, or forgotten, and let me see your face in them. Keep me close to you in the Eucharist and in prayer, even when you seem far away. Help me do small things with great love, faithfully and without seeking notice, until I come to you. Amen.
prayer.note: "Small things with great love" echoes a phrase widely associated with her; it is used here as an allusion, not a quotation.

link.label: Novena and prayers to St. Teresa of Calcutta (Mother Teresa Center)

feastCustoms: Attend Mass on September 5, the anniversary of her death in 1997; since 2025 it has been an optional memorial in the General Roman Calendar, so check whether your parish is keeping it.
Pray the nine-day Novena to St. Teresa of Calcutta published by the Mother Teresa Center, ending on the eve of her feast; one day's theme is Jesus' words "I thirst."
Pray the Memorare several times in a row, the so-called "flying novena" she was known to use in urgent needs (accounts differ on whether she prayed it nine or ten times).
Spend some time before the Blessed Sacrament, as she began each day with Jesus in the Eucharist.
Visit, feed, or sit with someone who is sick, elderly, or alone, or give time to a local shelter or care home; Pope Francis held her up as a model for volunteers.
mother-teresa.confirmationNote: St. Teresa of Calcutta can suit a Confirmation candidate who wants faith to show up in service. She was a teacher for nearly twenty years before answering a second call, which shows that God can redirect a life already given to him. She also kept praying through long years of spiritual darkness. Taking her name can mean committing to daily prayer and to noticing people others pass by.
reflectionPrompts: Who in your family, school, or neighborhood feels unwanted or overlooked, and how could you show them that they matter this week?
Choose one ordinary task you do every day and offer it to God as an act of love for a specific person in need.
Read Matthew 25:31–46 and John 19:25–30, then read the Holy See's biography of Mother Teresa and note how those two passages shaped her work.

padre-pio.heroSummary: St. Pio of Pietrelcina, widely known as Padre Pio, was an Italian Capuchin friar and priest who spent more than fifty years at San Giovanni Rotondo celebrating Mass, hearing confessions, and counseling crowds of visitors. Catholics keep his memorial on September 23. Beyond the reports of the stigmata, he left prayer groups and a hospital for the suffering.
padre-pio.searchDescription: St. Pio of Pietrelcina (Padre Pio), Capuchin priest of San Giovanni Rotondo known for the confessional, prayer groups and a hospital. Feast: September 23.

symbols.meaning: His vows as a Capuchin Franciscan friar, a life of poverty and prayer he embraced from 1903.

symbols.symbol: Fingerless gloves or mittens on the hands
symbols.meaning: He covered the wounds on his hands, disliking the attention they drew; surviving gloves are kept as relics.
The marks reported from September 1918, which the Church's prayer for his feast links to a share in Christ's Cross.
His Marian prayer; the National Centre for Padre Pio records that he died holding his rosary.

padre-pio.whyWeTurn: People turn to Padre Pio because his ministry was close to ordinary struggles. For decades he sat in the confessional for long hours, and visitors left feeling heard and forgiven. He prayed for those who asked, and the National Centre for Padre Pio notes that he recited a novena to the Sacred Heart every day for their intentions. Reports of the stigmata and other extraordinary gifts drew crowds and Church investigations, and he accepted restrictions without protest. Many find comfort in that patience under suffering. He also built something lasting: a hospital for the sick and prayer groups that still meet. To ask his prayers is to be pointed back to Christ, confession, and care for the suffering.

quotes.text: With Christ I am nailed to the cross. And I live, now not I; but Christ liveth in me.
But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ; by whom the world is crucified to me, and I to the world.

prayer.text: Lord Jesus Christ, you gave Saint Pio a deep love for your Cross, for the Mass, and for the sacrament of mercy. Through his prayers, give me the courage to bring my sins honestly to confession and to trust your forgiveness. When I suffer, keep me close to you without bitterness. Teach me to pray faithfully for others, as he did for all who asked, and open my eyes to the sick and lonely around me. May I pray, hope, and not lose heart, until I see your face. Amen.

link.label: Prayer to Saint Pio (National Centre for Padre Pio)

feastCustoms: Attend Mass on September 23, the obligatory memorial of St. Pio in the universal Roman calendar, and listen for its prayer about sharing in Christ's Cross.
Go to confession in the days around his feast, honoring the ministry he gave most of his hours to.
Pray the Efficacious Novena to the Sacred Heart of Jesus, which the National Centre for Padre Pio says he recited daily for those who asked his prayers.
Look for a Padre Pio Prayer Group near you; the groups began when he invited his spiritual children to pray together, and the Holy See approved their statute in 1986.

Do something for the sick, such as visiting someone in hospital or supporting a care facility, in the spirit of his Home for the Relief of Suffering; in San Giovanni Rotondo, the feast includes a procession with his statue.

padre-pio.confirmationNote: Padre Pio can suit a Confirmation candidate who wants to take prayer and confession seriously. His ministry was mostly quiet and repetitive: Mass, long hours hearing confessions, and counsel for people carrying heavy burdens. He also turned devotion into concrete help for the sick. Choosing his name can be a commitment to regular confession, faithful prayer for others, and patience when you are misunderstood.
reflectionPrompts: When did you last feel truly forgiven, and what might be keeping you from the sacrament of confession now?
Make a short list of people who have asked for your prayers, and pray for one of them by name each day this week.
Read Galatians 2:19–20 and 6:14, then read John Paul II's canonization homily for Padre Pio and note how it connects his life to the Cross.

paul-the-simple.heroSummary: St. Paul the Simple was an Egyptian peasant who, at about sixty, left a broken marriage and begged St. Anthony the Great to make him a monk. Anthony tested him hard and found him humble and obedient. Known for simplicity of heart, he is commemorated on March 7 by both Eastern and Western traditions.
paul-the-simple.searchDescription: St. Paul the Simple, fourth-century Egyptian hermit who became St. Anthony's disciple at about sixty, known for humble obedience. Feast: March 7.
paul-the-simple.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Paul the Simple because his story starts late and badly. He was an old farmer whose marriage had collapsed, and Anthony at first told him to go home. He waited at the door anyway. According to Palladius, when Anthony made him unpick a whole day's weaving and do it over, Paul neither complained nor grew angry. That patient obedience is why the desert fathers remembered him. Tradition holds that he later freed a man from an evil spirit that Anthony sent to him. Anyone who feels too old, too hurt, or too ordinary to begin again with God can find a friend in him.

quotes.text: It is impossible for me to die elsewhere than here.
quotes.work: Words attributed to Paul in Palladius, The Lausiac History 22.4

quotes.text: Amen I say to you, unless you be converted, and become as little children, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven.
Blessed are the clean of heart: for they shall see God.

prayer.text: Lord Jesus Christ, you welcomed Saint Paul the Simple when he came to you late in life, wounded and with nothing to offer but a willing heart. Through his prayers, give me the courage to begin again, whatever my age or my past. Teach me to accept correction without resentment, to redo patiently what I have done badly, and to trust you with a simple and undivided heart. Free me and those I love from every evil, and keep us humble before you. Amen.

feastCustoms: Remember him on March 7, the date on which Butler records that both Greeks and Latins commemorate him; in the current Roman calendar the day belongs to Sts. Perpetua and Felicity, so his memory is mostly a private devotion for Latin Catholics.
Eastern Orthodox and many Byzantine-tradition churches commemorate him on March 7 and again on October 4.
Read his short story in chapter 22 of Palladius's Lausiac History, a public-domain text from the desert tradition.
Redo one task you rushed or did poorly, carefully and without complaint, in memory of the mats Anthony had him unpick and weave again.
Pray a few psalms slowly in the evening, as Palladius describes Paul doing with Anthony.
paul-the-simple.confirmationNote: St. Paul the Simple can suit a Confirmation candidate who values humility and perseverance over talent. He came to faith seriously only in old age, after a painful betrayal, and was turned away before he was accepted. He stayed, learned, and did humble work without complaint. Choosing his name can mean committing to keep showing up for God, especially when it is hard or unglamorous.
reflectionPrompts: Is there a door you gave up knocking on, in prayer or in a relationship, that you might patiently knock on again?
The next time someone corrects your work this week, try to accept it calmly and redo the task without complaining.
Read chapter 22 of Palladius's Lausiac History (the story of Paul the Simple) alongside Matthew 18:1–4, and note what 'simplicity' means in each.

peter-julian-eymard.heroSummary: St. Peter Julian Eymard was a French priest known as the Apostle of the Eucharist. After serving as a diocesan priest and then a Marist, he founded the Congregation of the Blessed Sacrament in Paris in 1856 and, with Marguerite Guillot, the Servants of the Blessed Sacrament. Catholics remember him on August 2.
peter-julian-eymard.searchDescription: St. Peter Julian Eymard, the French priest called the Apostle of the Eucharist, founded the Congregation of the Blessed Sacrament in 1856. Feast: August 2.

symbols.meaning: Exposition of the Blessed Sacrament for adoration, the center of the religious communities he founded.
Christ's presence in the Eucharist, the heart of his spirituality and the reason he is called the Apostle of the Eucharist.
The vestment a priest wears for solemn exposition and Benediction, recalling his priestly ministry of leading people in adoration.
The veil a priest uses to hold the monstrance when blessing the people, a sign of reverence for the Real Presence.

peter-julian-eymard.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Peter Julian Eymard when they want to pray before the Blessed Sacrament and are not sure where to begin. He spent his life helping others discover Christ present in the Eucharist, first preaching Forty Hours devotions as a Marist, then founding communities devoted to adoration. He did not treat prayer as an escape: in Paris he prepared poor working people for First Communion and worked to improve their circumstances. He also wrote many letters guiding people in the spiritual life. Adorers, catechists, priests, and anyone whose prayer has gone dry find in him a patient guide who believed that time with Christ changes how we serve others.

quotes.text: And Jesus said to them: I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall not hunger: and he that believeth in me shall never thirst.
He that eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, abideth in me, and I in him.

prayer.text: Lord Jesus, truly present in the Most Holy Sacrament, you gave Saint Peter Julian Eymard a great love for your Eucharistic presence and a heart for the poor. Through his prayers, draw me to spend time with you in adoration, even when my prayer feels dry. Let what I receive at your altar overflow into patience, generosity, and practical care for the people around me. Bless priests, catechists, and all who prepare others to meet you in Holy Communion. Make me, like him, a friend who brings others to you. Amen.

feastCustoms: Attend Mass on August 2, his optional memorial in the General Roman Calendar, where John Paul II placed it in 1995.
Make a holy hour before the Blessed Sacrament, as Catholic Culture suggests for his day.
Learn about the Congregation of the Blessed Sacrament and the Servants of the Blessed Sacrament, the communities he founded for men and women.
Help someone prepare for First Communion or thank your parish catechists, recalling his work with poor working people in Paris.
If you are in Paris, pray at his tomb in the Chapelle Corpus Christi, where his relics were brought from La Mure in 1877.

places.name: Chapelle Corpus Christi (his tomb; Fathers of the Blessed Sacrament)

peter-julian-eymard.confirmationNote: St. Peter Julian Eymard can suit a Confirmation candidate who is drawn to the Eucharist, to adoration, or to teaching the faith. He helped poor workers in Paris prepare for First Communion and founded communities devoted to prayer before the Blessed Sacrament. Taking his name can mean committing to regular time with Christ in the Eucharist and letting that prayer shape how you serve others.
reflectionPrompts: When did you last spend unhurried time with Christ in the Blessed Sacrament, and what keeps you from doing it more often?
Sign up for an hour of adoration at a parish chapel this month, or offer to help with a First Communion class.
Read John 6:22–59 slowly, then read the Congregation of the Blessed Sacrament's account of his life and note how his Eucharistic devotion led to practical service.

philip-neri.heroSummary: St. Philip Neri was a sixteenth-century priest in Rome who drew people to God through friendship, prayer, care for the sick, and good humor. From the gatherings around him grew the Congregation of the Oratory, approved in 1575. Catholics keep his memorial on May 26, and many remember him for his cheerfulness.
philip-neri.searchDescription: St. Philip Neri, the joyful priest of Rome who founded the Congregation of the Oratory: his symbols, sayings, a prayer and his May 26 feast.

symbols.meaning: Recalls the experience his early biographers place just before Pentecost 1544 in the catacomb of San Sebastiano, when he felt a globe of fire enter his chest; the Church's prayer for his feast asks the Holy Spirit to kindle that same fire in us.
Purity of heart; Catholic Culture lists the lily among his traditional symbols and recalls his spotless youth in Florence.
His prayer to Mary; Catholic Culture lists the rosary among the attributes used for him.

symbols.symbol: Priestly vestments or the black cassock of the Oratory
symbols.meaning: His priesthood from 1551 and the Oratory he founded, a community of secular priests who live together without religious vows.

philip-neri.whyWeTurn: People turn to Philip Neri because his holiness feels approachable. Long before he was ordained, he visited the sick in Rome's hospitals, prayed through the night, and talked about God with anyone who wanted to listen. As a priest he heard confessions for long hours and used jokes to deflate vanity, including his own. He refused to make faith grim, teaching that cheerfulness helps a person persevere. He also tied prayer to service, saying it was better to answer a call for help than to stay in one's room praying. Many ask his prayers for honest joy, humility without gloom, and a heart set on fire by the Holy Spirit.

quotes.text: Rejoice in the Lord always; again, I say, rejoice.
Cheerfulness strengthens the heart and makes us persevere in a good life; wherefore the servant of God ought always to be in good spirits.
quotes.work: Maxims and Sayings of St. Philip Neri, January 7

quotes.text: Charity and cheerfulness, or charity and humility, should be our motto.
quotes.work: Maxims and Sayings of St. Philip Neri, April 25

prayer.text: Lord God, you set the heart of Saint Philip Neri on fire with your Holy Spirit and gave him a joy that drew others to you. Through his prayers, free me from the seriousness that is really pride and from the sadness that forgets your mercy. Teach me to laugh at myself, to listen well, and to set my plans aside when someone needs my help. Make me faithful in prayer, hungry for the Eucharist, and honest in confession. Let my friendships lead others toward you, as his did in the streets of Rome. Amen.

feastCustoms: Attend Mass on May 26, the memorial of St. Philip Neri in the universal Roman calendar; its opening prayer asks that the Holy Spirit kindle in us the fire that filled his heart.
Spend time before the Blessed Sacrament; Catholic Culture notes that Corpus Christi was his favorite feast, and he died on that feast in 1595.
Laugh at yourself the next time something annoys you, and make a point of cheering someone else up, as Catholic Culture suggests for his day.
Read one of his maxims and let it shape your day; the collection of his sayings was arranged for one short reading each day of the year.
In Rome, pilgrims still walk the roughly 25 km Seven Churches route that Philip began leading with large groups in 1559, and many visit his body at Santa Maria in Vallicella (the Chiesa Nuova).

places.name: Santa Maria in Vallicella (Chiesa Nuova), church of the Roman Oratory

philip-neri.confirmationNote: Philip Neri suits a Confirmation candidate who wants faith to feel like friendship rather than a performance. He took prayer, confession, and the Eucharist seriously, yet he was quick to laugh and slow to take himself too seriously. He also kept showing up for the sick and for anyone who knocked on his door. Choosing his name can be a commitment to joyful prayer, humility, and loyal friendship.
reflectionPrompts: Where has taking yourself too seriously crowded out joy, and what would it look like to laugh at your own vanity this week?
Choose one interruption tomorrow and treat it as Philip did, as a call to serve rather than an obstacle to your plans.
Read Philippians 4:4–7 in the Douay-Rheims and the January maxims in F. W. Faber's translation of the Maxims and Sayings of St. Philip Neri, and note which saying challenges you most.
