pier-giorgio-frassati.heroSummary: St. Pier Giorgio Frassati (1901–1925) was a Turin engineering student, mountaineer, and Lay Dominican who spent his free time visiting poor families through the St. Vincent de Paul Society. He died of polio at twenty-four, was beatified by John Paul II in 1990, and was canonized with Carlo Acutis in 2025. His feast is July 4.
pier-giorgio-frassati.searchDescription: St. Pier Giorgio Frassati (1901–1925), feast July 4: Turin student, mountaineer, and friend of the poor, canonized with Carlo Acutis in 2025.

symbols.symbol: Mountaineering gear: ice axe, rope, and climbing clothes
symbols.meaning: His lifelong love of the mountains as a member of the Club Alpino Italiano and Giovane Montagna; Pope Leo XIV recalled that his last photograph shows him climbing in the Val di Lanzo.
His Marian devotion, from the Piccoli Rosarianti as a boy to the Milites Mariae in his parish; EWTN recounts that he prayed the rosary daily, often kneeling by his bed.

symbols.symbol: Dominican scapular or habit of a tertiary
symbols.meaning: He received the habit of the Dominican Third Order in 1922, taking the name Fra Girolamo.

symbols.symbol: Bundles or a cart of supplies for the poor
symbols.meaning: His visits to poor families through the St. Vincent de Paul Society; friends joked that he ran a transport company, as Pope Leo XIV noted in the canonization homily.
His daily Communion, frequent confession, and membership in the Eucharistic League and the students' Nocturnal Adoration Society.

pier-giorgio-frassati.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Pier Giorgio Frassati because he loved life and gave it away freely. He climbed mountains, shared jokes and adventures with friends, studied engineering, and took a public stand for justice, yet he quietly spent his own money and time on poor families in Turin. Crowds of people he had quietly helped came to his funeral. Students, young adults, hikers, and anyone trying to live faith in the middle of a busy, social life find in him a cheerful companion. He shows that prayer, friendship, adventure, and service to the poor belong together, and that a short life can be a full one.

quotes.text: I have lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from whence help shall come to me. My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth.
Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy.
quotes.work: Matthew 5:7, from the Beatitudes; John Paul II called him a man of the Beatitudes

quotes.text: And whosoever doth not carry his cross and come after me, cannot be my disciple.
quotes.work: Luke 14:27, from the Gospel of his canonization Mass

prayer.text: Lord Jesus, you gave Saint Pier Giorgio a joyful heart, a love for the mountains, and eyes that saw you in the poor. Through his prayers, help me to keep you at the center of my days in the Eucharist, in confession, and in the rosary. Make me a loyal friend and a cheerful companion. Give me the courage to stand up for what is right and the generosity to give my time and my money to people in need, without seeking notice. Lead me upward, step by step, until I reach you. Amen.

feastCustoms: Keep his feast on July 4, the anniversary of his death; the Archdiocese of Turin celebrates it as his liturgical feast, and the Dominican family honors him as one of their own.
Go on a hike or climb with friends, and pray together at the top or along the trail.
Visit, call, or bring supplies to someone poor, sick, or alone, or volunteer with a St. Vincent de Paul Society conference in your parish.
Pray the rosary, which he prayed daily, or go to confession and a weekday Mass.
Read the short biography in the Holy See's canonization booklet and share one story about him with a friend.

places.name: Turin Cathedral (Cathedral of St. John the Baptist), where his remains rest; Archdiocese of Turin site

pier-giorgio-frassati.confirmationNote: St. Pier Giorgio Frassati suits a Confirmation candidate who loves the outdoors, sports, friendship, or working for justice. He was a fun-loving student who also went to daily Mass and spent his free hours with poor families. Choosing his name can mean committing to faith that shows up in action: serving people in need, standing for what is right, and inviting friends along.
reflectionPrompts: Who are the people in my town or school that most others overlook, and how could I quietly help one of them this month?
Plan an outing with friends, a hike, a game, or a meal, and include a moment of prayer or a visit to someone in need.
Read Matthew 5:1–12 in the Douay-Rheims, then read his biography in the Holy See's 2025 canonization booklet and match each Beatitude to something he did.

scholastica.heroSummary: St. Scholastica was the sister of St. Benedict and, in Gregory the Great's words, dedicated to God from her infancy. Almost all we know comes from two short chapters of Gregory's Dialogues: a prayer that brought down a storm, and Benedict's vision of her soul rising as a dove. Her feast is February 10.
scholastica.searchDescription: St. Scholastica, sister of St. Benedict, is honored February 10. Gregory the Great tells of her storm-bringing prayer and her soul rising as a dove.

symbols.meaning: Gregory's account that Benedict saw her soul ascend to heaven in the likeness of a dove three days after their last meeting; art sometimes shows the dove leaving her mouth.
Her role, in Benedictine tradition, as head of a community of women near Montecassino; Gregory himself does not describe her as an abbess.
A life consecrated to Christ, which Gregory says began in her infancy.
Her consecrated virginity; the Church keeps her feast as the memorial of St. Scholastica, Virgin.

scholastica.whyWeTurn: People turn to St. Scholastica because her one remembered conversation is so human. She had a brother she saw once a year, she wanted one more night of talking about God with him, and when he said no, she prayed. Gregory the Great, who tells the story, takes her side: she could do more, he says, because she loved more. Nuns and Benedictine communities honor her as a mother of their way of life, and tradition invokes her against storms and lightning. Brothers and sisters, close friends, and anyone who longs for deeper conversation about faith find in her a patient, loving intercessor.

quotes.text: I desired you to stay, and you would not hear me, I have desired our good Lord, and he hath vouchsafed to grant my petition: wherefore if you can now depart, in God's name return to your monastery, and leave me here alone.
quotes.work: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book II, chapter 33 (Scholastica's words to Benedict, as Gregory reports them)
quotes.translation: P. W. (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (London: Philip Lee Warner, 1911; public domain)

quotes.text: ...according to the saying of St. John, God is charity and therefore of right she did more which loved more.
quotes.work: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book II, chapter 33 (Gregory writing about Scholastica)
quotes.translation: P. W. (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (London: Philip Lee Warner, 1911; public domain)

quotes.text: ...as their souls were always one in God whiles they lived, so their bodies continued together after their death.
quotes.work: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book II, chapter 34 (on her burial in Benedict's own grave)
quotes.translation: P. W. (1608), ed. Edmund G. Gardner (London: Philip Lee Warner, 1911; public domain)

prayer.text: Lord God, St. Scholastica gave her life to you from childhood and loved to speak with her brother about the joys of heaven. Through her prayers, teach us to pray with the trust of a child who knows she will be heard. Bless our brothers and sisters, our families and our friendships, and make our conversations places where you are welcome. Give us hearts that love much, so that, like her, we may desire you above all things and one day rejoice with her in your presence. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

feastCustoms: Attend Mass on February 10, the memorial of St. Scholastica, Virgin, in the General Roman Calendar.
Read Gregory the Great's Dialogues, Book II, chapters 33 and 34, the short account of her last visit with Benedict.
Call, write to or visit a brother, sister or close friend, and talk about something that matters to your faith.
With children, tell the story of the "holy twins" Benedict and Scholastica and make a paper dove for a window or home altar.
Try lectio divina, the slow, prayerful reading of Scripture at the heart of Benedictine life, for a few minutes of the day.

places.name: Abbey of Montecassino

scholastica.confirmationNote: Scholastica suits a confirmand who prays with confidence and treasures the people who share their faith. Her story is a reminder that prayer is real conversation with a God who listens, and that love can be bold. Confirmation strengthens Christians to live and witness to Christ; Scholastica shows that this witness can grow quietly, through faithful prayer, a consecrated heart and loving friendship.
reflectionPrompts: Who in my life do I most want to talk with about God, and when did I last do it?
Set aside ten minutes today to bring one specific request to God with the confidence Scholastica showed.
Read Gregory the Great's Dialogues, Book II, chapters 33–34, and ask why Gregory says she "did more which loved more".

Benedictine abbess who brought women's monastic life to Germany
Benedictine abbess and later daughter of the tradition Scholastica began
Led women in the way of life of another founder, Francis

teresa-of-avila.heroSummary: St. Teresa of Ávila (1515–1582), also called Teresa of Jesus, was a Spanish Carmelite who founded St. Joseph's in Ávila in 1562 and began a reform built on small, prayerful communities. Her Life, Way of Perfection, and Interior Castle still teach prayer as friendship with God. Her feast is October 15.
teresa-of-avila.searchDescription: St. Teresa of Ávila (1515–1582), feast October 15: Carmelite reformer, author of the Interior Castle, and the first woman named a Doctor of the Church.

symbols.symbol: Heart pierced by an angel's fiery spear
symbols.meaning: In her Life (chapter 29) she describes an angel thrusting a golden spear tipped with fire into her heart, leaving her on fire with love of God; Carmelites commemorate it as the Transverberation.
Her writings on prayer and religious life, the basis for Paul VI naming her a Doctor of the Church in 1970.
The Holy Spirit as the source of her teaching; in her Life (chapter 38) she also describes seeing a dove above her head during prayer.
The brown habit and white mantle of the reformed Carmelite communities she founded, beginning with St. Joseph's in Ávila.

teresa-of-avila.whyWeTurn: People turn to Teresa when prayer feels dry, distracted, or impossible. She struggled for years to pray well, and she wrote about it with humor and frankness, describing prayer as friendship with the One who loves us. She was also practical: she founded houses, managed scarce resources, traveled hard roads, and faced opposition. Tradition holds that she kept a short poem in her breviary reminding her that God alone suffices. Catholics ask her prayers for perseverance, for the sick, and for those discerning religious life. She shows that contemplation and hard work belong together, and that love of neighbor is the test of prayer.

quotes.text: mental prayer is nothing else, in my opinion, but being on terms of friendship with God, frequently conversing in secret with Him Who, we know, loves us.
quotes.work: The Life of St. Teresa of Jesus, chapter 8

quotes.text: The soul is satisfied now with nothing less than God.
quotes.work: The Life of St. Teresa of Jesus, chapter 29

prayer.source: St. Teresa of Ávila, "Nada te turbe" (Santa Teresa's Book-Mark), translated by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, Complete Poetical Works (public domain)
prayer.note: Longfellow's subtitle records the tradition that she carried this short poem as a bookmark in her breviary; Catholic Culture also presents it as hers. Many modern translations word it differently ("Let nothing disturb you..."). The popular prayer "Christ has no body now but yours" is often credited to Teresa, but it is not found in her known writings.

link.label: Longfellow's Complete Poetical Works at Project Gutenberg

feastCustoms: Attend Mass on October 15, her memorial in the General Roman Calendar; Carmelite communities celebrate their foundress with higher rank.
Copy her bookmark prayer by hand and keep it in your Bible or prayer book.
Spend fifteen minutes in quiet mental prayer, speaking to Christ simply, as to a friend.
Read a chapter of her Life or the first dwelling places of the Interior Castle.
Make a Spanish treat such as yemas de Santa Teresa, the egg-yolk sweets associated with Ávila.
teresa-of-avila.confirmationNote: Teresa suits a Confirmation candidate who wants a real relationship with God and is honest that prayer can be hard. She also fits someone with energy and plans, since she was a founder and organizer as well as a teacher of prayer. Choosing her means committing to regular personal prayer, measuring it by growth in charity, and persevering when feelings fade.
reflectionPrompts: If prayer is friendship with God, what kind of friend have I been to him lately?
Each day this week, spend ten minutes talking to Jesus in your own words, then do one kindness that interrupts your plans.
Read chapter 8 of her Life in David Lewis's translation, where she describes mental prayer as friendship with God.

Franciscan reformer who counseled and encouraged her, as she recounts in her Life
Read Teresa's autobiography in one night, became a Carmelite, and took the name Teresa
Declared a Doctor of the Church one week after Teresa in 1970

therese-of-lisieux.heroSummary: St. Thérèse of Lisieux was a French Carmelite nun who died in 1897 at twenty-four and is now a Doctor of the Church. Her "little way" teaches confidence in God's merciful love within ordinary duties. Named a patron of missions in 1927 without ever leaving her convent, she is celebrated on October 1.
therese-of-lisieux.searchDescription: St. Thérèse of Lisieux (1873–1897) was a French Carmelite and Doctor of the Church. Explore her little way, October 1 feast, and patronage of missions.

symbols.meaning: Her hope, recorded by her sisters, to let fall a shower of roses after her death; devotees see them as a sign of her intercession.
Her love for Christ crucified and her offering of herself to God's merciful love in 1895; she is often shown holding a crucifix together with roses.

symbols.symbol: Brown Carmelite habit with white mantle
symbols.meaning: Her life as a Discalced Carmelite nun in the monastery at Lisieux, which she entered at fifteen.

symbols.symbol: The Child Jesus and the Holy Face
symbols.meaning: Her religious name, Thérèse of the Child Jesus and of the Holy Face, joining trust like a child's with devotion to the suffering Christ.

therese-of-lisieux.whyWeTurn: People turn to Thérèse when they feel small. She did not found an order, travel as a missionary, or write theology in a university, yet the Church calls her a Doctor. Her little way says that holiness begins with trust in God's mercy and grows through ordinary acts of love done well. She is honest company in hard times, too: her last illness came with a long trial of faith, and she kept choosing trust without feeling consolation. Many Catholics ask her prayers for missionaries, for vocations, and for the courage to love in small, hidden ways. Tradition holds that she answers with roses, but her deeper gift is confidence.

quotes.text: I will seek out a means of getting to Heaven by a little way--very short and very straight, a little way that is wholly new.
quotes.work: Story of a Soul, Chapter IX

quotes.text: With me prayer is an uplifting of the heart; a glance towards heaven; a cry of gratitude and love, uttered equally in sorrow and in joy.
quotes.work: Story of a Soul, Chapter X

quotes.text: O Jesus, my Love, at last I have found my vocation. My vocation is love! Yes, I have found my place in the bosom of the Church, and this place, O my God, Thou hast Thyself given to me: in the heart of the Church, my Mother, I will be LOVE!
quotes.work: Story of a Soul, Chapter XI

prayer.text: Merciful Father, you taught St. Thérèse to come to you with the trust of a little child. Through her prayers, free me from the need to prove myself, and help me to receive your love as a gift. Show me the small, hidden acts of love I can offer today, in my family, my work and my prayer. Sustain the missionaries who carry the Gospel far from home, and keep me faithful when faith feels dark. Let my life, like hers, become love in the heart of your Church. Amen.

link.label: Prayer times at the Sanctuary of Lisieux

feastCustoms: Attend Mass on October 1, her memorial in the universal calendar.
Pray a nine-day novena ending on September 30, the anniversary of her death; many people bring roses to her image as they pray.
Pray for a missionary by name, or support one, in honor of her patronage of the missions.
Read one chapter of Story of a Soul and choose one small act of love to practice that day.
In Lisieux, the Teresian festivals on the weekend before September 30 include a torchlight procession with her relics.

therese-of-lisieux.confirmationNote: Thérèse suits a candidate who feels ordinary and wonders whether holiness is really meant for them. Her life shows that faith can grow through small faithful choices, honest prayer, and trust when feelings are absent. She is also a good choice for someone who wants to support the Church's mission through prayer and service right where they already live.
reflectionPrompts: Where do I try to earn God's love instead of receiving it, and what would trusting him look like there?
Choose one hidden act of kindness each day this week that no one will notice or thank you for.
Read Chapter IX of Story of a Soul (Taylor translation) alongside Proverbs 9:4 and Isaias 66:12–13 in the Douay-Rheims, the passages she used to explain her little way.

thomas-aquinas.heroSummary: St. Thomas Aquinas is the patron saint of Catholic schools, a title Pope Leo XIII gave him in 1880. A Dominican friar and Doctor of the Church, he taught that faith and reason work together, wrote the Summa Theologiae, and died at Fossanova in 1274. His feast is January 28.
thomas-aquinas.searchDescription: St. Thomas Aquinas (c. 1225–1274), feast January 28: Dominican Doctor of the Church, author of the Summa Theologiae, and patron of Catholic schools.

symbols.meaning: The light of his teaching, which helped illuminate the Church's understanding of the faith.
His student nickname, the "dumb ox," given to a large, quiet young friar; tradition adds that Albert the Great predicted this ox would one day be heard throughout the world.
His devotion to the Eucharist and the Corpus Christi texts traditionally credited to him, including the Pange Lingua and Adoro te devote.

symbols.symbol: Teaching, with pagan philosophers at his feet
symbols.meaning: His work as a master in the universities and his use of thinkers such as Aristotle in the service of Christian truth.
His life as a friar of the Order of Preachers and his enormous body of writing, above all the Summa Theologiae.

thomas-aquinas.whyWeTurn: Students have long asked St. Thomas for help before exams and papers, and that is a fine place to start. But he offers more than better grades. He was a patient, careful thinker who took hard questions seriously, listened to opponents, and believed that honest reasoning can lead toward God rather than away from him. He also prayed before the crucifix and the Blessed Sacrament, and tradition holds that near the end of his life he said that all he had written seemed like straw beside what God had shown him. We turn to him when we need clear thinking, humility about what we know, and a faith that is not afraid of questions.

quotes.text: Since therefore grace does not destroy nature but perfects it, natural reason should minister to faith as the natural bent of the will ministers to charity.

quotes.text: Hence it was necessary for the salvation of man that certain truths which exceed human reason should be made known to him by divine revelation.

prayer.text: Lord God, you gave St. Thomas Aquinas a great love for truth and a heart that bowed before the mystery of the Eucharist. Open my mind when I study, and keep me humble about what I know. Help me to ask good questions, to listen fairly to others, and to follow the truth wherever it leads. When learning is hard, give me patience; when it goes well, keep me grateful. Through St. Thomas's prayers, bless all students, teachers, and Catholic schools, and let everything I learn bring me closer to you. Amen.
prayer.note: The Adoro te devote is traditionally attributed to St. Thomas. Gerard Manley Hopkins's English version ("Godhead here in hiding") exists in several drafts with differing wording, so it is linked rather than reproduced here.

thomas-aquinas.confirmationNote: Thomas suits a candidate who loves learning, asks a lot of questions, or wonders whether faith and science can fit together. He chose his vocation against his family's wishes and gave his intelligence to God rather than to ambition. Choosing him can be a commitment to study the faith seriously, to think honestly, and to keep prayer at the center of learning.
reflectionPrompts: What question about faith do I usually avoid, and what might it look like to bring it honestly to God and to people I trust?
Before you study this week, pause for one minute to offer the work to God and ask for clear thinking.
Read Summa Theologiae I, question 1, article 1, in the English Dominican translation, then Benedict XVI's June 2, 2010 audience on St. Thomas.

toribio-romo-gonz-lez.heroSummary: St. Toribio Romo González is a Mexican priest and martyr whom many migrants invoke as a patron of immigrants, a popular devotion that grew from the 1970s. Born in Jalisco in 1900, he served the parish of Tequila during the persecution of the 1920s and was shot on February 25, 1928. He was canonized in 2000.
toribio-romo-gonz-lez.whyWeTurn: Many migrants and their families turn to Santo Toribio before a dangerous journey north. Catholic News Service reports that stories of his help began circulating in the 1970s, some describing him appearing to travelers in need; these are popular accounts, not events the Church has examined. The documented man was a young parish priest who kept celebrating the sacraments while in hiding, prayed never to let a day pass without Mass, and offered his life for peace in the Church. People who feel far from home, unsafe, or uncertain find in him a priest who stayed with his people. To ask his prayers is to entrust the journey, and those who make it, to Christ.

quotes.text: Greater love than this no man hath, that a man lay down his life for his friends.
He that eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, abideth in me, and I in him.
For I was hungry, and you gave me to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me to drink; I was a stranger, and you took me in.

prayer.text: Lord Jesus, you gave Saint Toribio Romo a love for the Eucharist so deep that he begged never to spend a day without offering Mass. Through his prayers, protect all who leave home in search of safety or work, and those who wait and worry for them. Give them good people along the way, and give me the courage to welcome the stranger as I would welcome you. Strengthen priests who serve under threat, and keep me close to you in the Eucharist, whatever road I travel. Amen.

feastCustoms: Attend Mass on May 21, when the Church remembers St. Christopher Magallanes and companions, the martyrs of Mexico's persecution, Toribio among them.
On February 25, the anniversary of his death, pray for priests and Christians who serve under threat.
Pray for migrants and their families, and support a parish or Catholic ministry that welcomes them; near his sanctuary in Jalisco, a migrant house named for him shelters travelers.
Go to a weekday Mass or spend time before the Blessed Sacrament, remembering his prayer never to spend a day without celebrating Mass.
In Santa Ana de Guadalupe, Jalisco, his hometown, pilgrims visit the sanctuary where he is buried to give thanks and ask his prayers.
toribio-romo-gonz-lez.confirmationNote: Toribio Romo suits a Confirmation candidate who cares about migrants and refugees, or whose own family knows what it is to leave home. He was an ordinary parish priest who loved the Mass, kept the parish records up to date, and stayed with his people when it was dangerous. Choosing his name can be a commitment to courage, love for the Eucharist, and practical welcome for those far from home.
reflectionPrompts: Who in your family or community has left home to start again, and how can you hold them in prayer this week?
Find out what a local parish or Catholic agency does for migrants, and offer time, supplies, or a donation.
Read Matthew 25:31–46 in the Douay-Rheims, then the Vatican's biography of Toribio Romo González, and note how his last night connects to ordinary parish service.
